## docs/Reference/Core/Implements.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1066331884382072912, 1086882000025178112, 1305613804180209785, 1477515216680911000, 1243608396150603838, 1397159152203206656, 1484135023694184560, 1491034044325036173, 1208962924820045896, 1386545607916912720, 1478113080419418213]

### Implements WithEvents ... Via

A class can both implement an interface and forward that interface's events to outside consumers by combining the `WithEvents` and `Via` modifiers:

```tb
Implements WithEvents InterfaceName Via memberVariable
```

The member variable named after `Via` must itself be declared `WithEvents` inside the class. This lets a `WithEvents` variable typed as the interface receive events raised by whichever concrete object is assigned to `memberVariable` at runtime --- making it possible to swap implementations (for example, `StdIO` versus `NamedPipeIO`) while event-handler code written against the interface remains unchanged.

An example from the twinBASIC runtime source (`ActiveXExtender.twin`):

```tb
Implements WithEvents T Via ClientObject
```

where `T` is the interface type parameter and `ClientObject` is the `WithEvents`-declared member.

> [!NOTE]
> A known compiler limitation requires at least one `Event` declaration to be present in the class body for the `WithEvents Implements Via` to be included in the compiled output. Without any `Event` on the class, the forwarded events from the interface are silently dropped. A dummy event declaration works around this until the limitation is resolved:
>
> ```tb
> Event xIgnored()  ' Required by compiler until limitation is resolved.
> ```

_Source threads: 1391490480432349346 · confidence: high_

> [!NOTE]
> When a class uses `Implements ClassName`, twinBASIC generates an implicit field inside the implementing class with the same name as the implemented class. This field starts as **Nothing** and must be set explicitly if the class intends to delegate to another instance. Accessing this auto-generated field is unusual; the compiler emits a warning --- *"Unusual use of implicit field generated from an Implements statement"* --- when it is referenced. The warning does not prevent compilation. This behavior matches VB6.

> [!NOTE]
> When a derived class inherits a base class that already implements an interface, the derived class does not need to re-declare the implementation --- inherited interface members are available automatically unless the derived class overrides them. However, if the derived class needs to implement a second interface that extends the first, there is no syntax to instruct the compiler to use the base class's existing implementation for the shared portion. The only workaround is to add forwarding methods in the derived class that delegate to the inherited implementations. This delegation shorthand is planned for a future release.

## docs/Reference/Core/Implements.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1066331884382072912, 1086882000025178112, 1305613804180209785, 1477515216680911000, 1391490480432349346, 1243608396150603838, 1397159152203206656, 1484135023694184560, 1491034044325036173, 1208962924820045896, 1478113080419418213]

### COM implementation gotchas

Two pitfalls arise specifically when implementing COM interfaces that the Windows OS calls back into:

**Uninitialized `[out]` parameters.** When the OS calls an interface method and passes a `ByRef ppObject As ISomeInterface` that is semantically write-only (an `[out]` parameter), the incoming value is not guaranteed to be `Nothing` --- it may contain a junk (uninitialized) pointer. A plain `Set ppObject = New SomeClass` will first attempt to release the original value of `ppObject`, which dereferences the junk pointer and crashes. Zero the pointer before the assignment:

```tb
PutMemPtr VarPtr(ppObject), vbNullPtr
Set ppObject = New SomeClass
```

This is different from a twinBASIC-to-twinBASIC call, where the compiler can sanitize callers automatically; when the caller is the OS, no such guarantee exists.

**`QueryInterface` with the same source and destination variable.** Calling `QueryInterface` and passing the same variable for both the input and output produces a reference leak:

```tb
' Wrong -- leaks the original reference:
ppObject.QueryInterface(IID_IFoo, ppObject)
```

The `QueryInterface` implementation overwrites the output variable without releasing the old reference stored there. Use a separate, initially-Nothing destination variable:

```tb
Dim pFoo As IFoo
ppObject.QueryInterface(IID_IFoo, pFoo)
Set ppObject = pFoo
```

_Source threads: 1386545607916912720 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-06-25 to 2025-06-26_
_Reviewer note: These gotchas apply to implementing any Windows COM interface (IShellFolder, IPropertyStore, etc.), not just twinBASIC-defined ones. Verify that PutMemPtr is the canonical pattern used in the community (vs. ZeroMemory or CopyMemory). The IID_IFoo placeholder in the QueryInterface example should be replaced with whatever the docs convention is for GUID arguments._

## docs/Reference/Core/Interface.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1071135379975057469, 1071135379975057469, 1071686119554568255, 1129802433158189086, 1281475744492687465, 1392099515309359114]

> [!NOTE]
> **`[ComImport(Boolean)]` and COM registration.** When a compiled twinBASIC binary (OCX or DLL) is registered, twinBASIC calls a custom `RegisterTypeLib` implementation that walks each `Interface` declaration and decides whether to write its IID into the registry. The `[ComImport(Boolean)]` attribute controls this decision. It accepts a **Boolean** argument and defaults to `True` for every `Interface` block.
>
> The `True` default is deliberate. On pre-UAC systems (Windows XP and earlier) an unregistered DLL attempts to delete the corresponding registry keys on unregistration. If a project redefines a system interface such as `IShellView`, a `False` default would cause unregistration to delete the live system key, potentially corrupting the OS. With `[ComImport(True)]`, registration is attempted but skipped gracefully when the key is protected; unregistration is a no-op for that entry.
>
> Without this behaviour (present before BETA 243), `RegisterTypeLib` raised a `TYPE_E_REGISTRYACCESS` error when any interface GUID matched a protected system registry key --- for example, when a `UserControl` implemented `IShellFolderViewDual`, `IShellView2`, or `IFolderView2`. VB6 avoided this silently because its `oleaut32` import was shimmed by `aclayers.dll`, which ignored write failures on protected keys and returned `S_OK` regardless.
>
> Set `[ComImport(False)]` explicitly on a brand-new interface that the project defines entirely itself and that should never be written to (or removed from) the system registry.

> [!NOTE]
> **`[OleAutomation(False)]` does not suppress registration for dual interfaces.** Applying `[OleAutomation(False)]` to an interface that `Extends IDispatch` (a dual interface) does not prevent `RegisterTypeLib` from attempting to register it. The `OleAutomation` flag is honoured only for pure dispatch-only interfaces (`dispinterface`). For dual interfaces the standard `RegisterTypeLib` ignores the flag and proceeds with registration regardless. Use `[ComImport(True)]` (the default) to handle protected-key failures gracefully instead.

_Source threads: 1071135379975057469 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-02-03 to 2023-02-06_
_Reviewer note: The current page documents `[ComImport]` as a flag only (no boolean argument, line 45). The findings indicate it takes `[ComImport(Boolean)]` with `True` as the default. Verify the exact attribute syntax against the twinBASIC compiler source or BETA 243 release notes before publishing. Also check whether `[ComImport]` (no argument) is still accepted as shorthand for `[ComImport(True)]`._

## docs/Reference/Core/Interface.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1071135379975057469, 1071135379975057469, 1071686119554568255, 1129802433158189086, 1281475744492687465, 1392099515309359114]

> [!NOTE]
> **`VARIANT_BOOL` mapping and `VARIANT_TRUE`.** The Windows SDK defines `VARIANT_BOOL` as `typedef short VARIANT_BOOL` --- a 2-byte signed integer. Mapping it to `Integer` in an interface member signature is therefore type-size-correct. However, `Boolean` is the semantically preferred type and the one COM infrastructure expects. More importantly, `VARIANT_TRUE` is `-1` (all bits set), not `1`. Interface implementations that return `1` for a true result are incorrect according to the COM specification and may cause misbehavior in COM consumers that check for the canonical `VARIANT_TRUE` value. Always return **True** (which twinBASIC emits as `-1`) rather than a literal `1`.

## docs/Reference/Core/LSet.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1111237398291021934]

> [!NOTE]
> The raw-memory-copy behavior of **LSet** between differently-typed UDTs applies only to *simple* UDTs --- those whose fields are all fixed-size numeric types. When a UDT contains `String`, `Object`, `Variant`, or dynamic-array fields, **LSet** copies each field individually using the same semantics as a normal assignment, not a raw byte copy. As a result, assigning an `Object` field from one UDT into a `Long` field of another via **LSet** does not extract the raw pointer value; the runtime applies field-level type rules instead.

## docs/Reference/Core/LeftShift.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> VB6 has no explicit bit-shift operators, so code written for VB6 sometimes multiplies or divides by powers of two (`i * 2`, `i * &H4`) to perform a logical shift, relying on the compiler's optimizer to emit a shift instruction. In twinBASIC, using **\<\<** and **\>\>** directly is preferred---it is clearer in intent and does not depend on optimizer behaviour.

## docs/Reference/Core/New.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1110498079972540436, 1291608868673294336, 1145039659911622656, 1357331478786080972, 1357675256252469454, 1468031072448020706]

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC supports parameterized constructors. A class can define `Public Sub New(Param1 As Type, ...)`, and instances are then created with `Set obj = New ClassName(arg1, arg2)`. VBA has no equivalent --- VBA code must use a factory method pattern instead.
>
> A class that is COM-creatable (the default) must also expose a parameterless `Public Sub New()` alongside any parameterized constructor, because COM requires that COM-creatable classes be instantiable without parameters. Defining only a parameterized constructor on a COM-creatable class causes a compilation error. To remove this constraint, mark the class `[COMCreatable(False)]`; the class can then expose only the parameterized constructor, but it cannot be created by COM clients outside twinBASIC.

## docs/Reference/Core/New.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1086699374073085992, 1291608868673294336, 1145039659911622656, 1357331478786080972, 1357675256252469454, 1468031072448020706]

> [!NOTE]
> When a COM type library marks a class with `TYPEFLAG_FCONTROL` (the ActiveX control flag), twinBASIC treats it as an ActiveX control. Declaring such a class by its coclass name (e.g. `Dim sc As MSScriptControl.ScriptControl`) and instantiating it with **New** causes the compiler to substitute the generated ActiveX wrapper interface for the declared type. Because the object is created directly with **New** rather than placed on a form, it is not wrapped in twinBASIC's ActiveX extender and does not support that wrapper interface --- producing a runtime `E_NOINTERFACE` / "No such interface supported" error at assignment. `MSScriptControl.ScriptControl` exhibits this behavior; the same code works in VB6 only when added via the References dialog, not the Components (ActiveX controls) dialog.
>
> Two fixes are available:
>
> - **Project Settings fix (permanent):** in Project Settings, turn off the "Use ActiveX Controls" flag for the reference, save, and restart the compiler. twinBASIC then treats the class as a plain COM reference and the coclass declaration works normally.
> - **Declaration workaround:** declare the variable as the class's default interface rather than the coclass name (`Dim sc As IScriptControl`). The **New** expression on the right-hand side still creates the object correctly; only the variable's declared type needs to be the interface:
>
>   ```tb
>   Dim sc As IScriptControl
>   Set sc = New MSScriptControl.ScriptControl
>   ```

> [!NOTE]
> When a class has both a `New` constructor (a twinBASIC addition) and a `Class_Initialize` or `Form_Initialize` event handler, the `New` constructor executes first, then `Initialize` fires. Both still fire --- neither suppresses the other. This ordering matters when a class has its predeclared ID set to `True`, because the default instance is created at application startup: code that relies on field values set in `Initialize` may run before the constructor has had a chance to supply them.

## docs/Reference/Core/New.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1086699374073085992, 1110498079972540436, 1291608868673294336, 1145039659911622656, 1357675256252469454, 1468031072448020706]

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC supports overloaded `Sub New(...)` constructors, but two limitations apply:
>
> **Parameter types:** Overload resolution fails when any overloaded `New` signature uses `Object` or `Variant` as a parameter type. These types prevent the overload discriminator from distinguishing candidates. Wrapping the ambiguous value in a `Type` (UDT) is the recommended workaround.
>
> **No constructor chaining:** There is no syntax to call one overloaded constructor from another (as C# allows via `this(...)`). Attempting it produces compile errors. Extract shared initialisation logic into a private method and call it from each overloaded constructor instead.

> [!NOTE]

Wrapping in parentheses, `(New ClassName(args)).Method`, parses but fails at runtime with error 438 (Object doesn't support this property or method). A common workaround is to define a module-level factory function with the same name as the class:
>
> ```tb
> Function MyClass(ByVal Name As String) As MyClass
>     Set MyClass = New MyClass(Name)
> End Function
> ```
>
> This enables the `MyClass("foo").Method` fluent pattern without assigning the object to a variable first.

## docs/Reference/Core/New.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1086699374073085992, 1110498079972540436, 1291608868673294336, 1145039659911622656, 1357331478786080972, 1357675256252469454]

## Parameterized constructors

A class can declare a **Sub** named **New** with one or more parameters to act as a parameterized constructor. The twinBASIC runtime invokes this **Sub** automatically when the class is created with **New**, passing the arguments from the **New** expression:

```tb
' Declaration (in the class body):
Private Sub New(ByVal title As String, ByVal width As Long)
    Caption = title
    Me.Width = width
End Sub

' Creation (at the call site):
Dim w As New MyWindow("Settings", 4000)
' or:
Set w = New MyWindow("Settings", 4000)
```

> [!NOTE]
> The access modifier on `Sub New` can be **Private** (or any other modifier). Declaring it **Private** prevents external code from calling it as a regular method while still allowing the **New** expression to invoke it normally. The `Sub New` declaration can appear anywhere in the class body.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> When a class defines a parameterized `Sub New`, the **Class_Initialize** event is never raised for that class --- the two mechanisms are mutually exclusive. Removing the `Sub New` declaration restores **Class_Initialize** behaviour. If initialisation logic must be shared, call the relevant code from inside `Sub New` explicitly; **Class_Initialize** will not fire automatically.

_Source threads: 1468031072448020706 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2026-02-02 to 2026-02-03_

## docs/Reference/Core/On-Error.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1113589601232240741, 1351545697060524033, 1478843597578174514]

> [!NOTE]
> When a runtime error occurs and no error handler is active, the procedure exits at that point. The exit is silent---no dialog appears and no further statements in the procedure run. Output produced before the error is retained, but any output that would have followed is silently omitted. This can make a logic error appear as unexpected early termination or missing results rather than an obvious error. Adding an `On Error GoTo` handler that logs `Err.Number` and `Err.Description` is the most reliable way to diagnose such failures.

## docs/Reference/Core/On-Error.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1201183841113612419, 1113589601232240741, 1478843597578174514]

> [!NOTE]
> When execution has entered an error-handling block --- that is, after an `On Error GoTo <label>` has fired and the labelled handler is running --- issuing a new `On Error GoTo <label2>` statement has no effect. The runtime considers itself still in error-handling mode and silently ignores the new handler. To install a fresh handler from inside an error-handling block, first exit error-handling mode:
>
> - `Resume <label>` transfers execution to a non-error path and leaves error-handling mode as a side effect.
> - `On Error GoTo -1` clears the current error object and resets error-handling mode without requiring a `Resume`. A subsequent `On Error GoTo <label>` then takes effect normally.
>
> `Err.Clear` alone is not sufficient --- it clears the **Err** object's properties but does not reset error-handling mode.

## docs/Reference/Core/On-Error.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1201183841113612419, 1113589601232240741, 1351545697060524033]

> [!NOTE]
> **On Error GoTo** is scoped to the procedure in which it appears and does not need to be reset with `On Error GoTo 0` before the procedure returns. However, `On Error Resume Next` used inside a called procedure without a matching `On Error GoTo 0` (or `Err.Clear`) before returning will leave the `Err` object in a non-zero state. The calling procedure's error handler may then read a stale error number from the nested call rather than from any new error that occurs afterward. Always pair `On Error Resume Next` with `On Error GoTo 0` or `Err.Clear` before the procedure exits.

## docs/Reference/Core/Open.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1507748304254140446, 1497886847886426285]

> [!NOTE]
> When no **Encoding** clause is given, the **Open** statement reads and writes text using the system ANSI code page. Files that contain characters outside the system ANSI range --- for example, UTF-8 encoded Chinese, Japanese, or other multibyte text --- appear as garbled characters unless the correct encoding is specified. Specify the encoding on the **Open** line to read such files correctly:
>
> ```tb
> Open "C:\MyFile.txt" For Input Encoding utf_8 As #1
> ```
>
> The **Encoding** argument also accepts a **String** variable, so a detected encoding can be passed dynamically.

## docs/Reference/Core/Open.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1422148580512104520, 1497886847886426285]

> [!NOTE]
> The `utf_8` and `utf_8_bom` encoding identifiers have distinct runtime behaviour and are not interchangeable. When a file begins with a UTF-8 byte-order mark (BOM, U+FEFF) and is opened with `Encoding utf_8`, the runtime does not strip the BOM before returning the first line or field; the BOM bytes appear at the start of the first value read, which causes numeric conversion functions such as `CLng()` to raise a Type Mismatch error on that value. Subsequent reads are unaffected. When a file begins with a BOM and is opened with `Encoding utf_8_bom`, the runtime consumes the BOM and the first read returns clean data. Conversely, opening a BOM-less file with `Encoding utf_8_bom` raises a runtime error (HRESULT 80004005) immediately on the `Open` statement. Programs that receive files of unknown provenance should attempt `Open ... Encoding utf_8_bom` first; if that raises an error, reopen with `Encoding utf_8`.

_Source threads: 1507748304254140446 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2026-05-23 to 2026-05-24_

## docs/Reference/Core/Open.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1422148580512104520, 1507748304254140446]

> [!NOTE]
> In **Binary** mode, **String** members inside UDTs are read and written using ANSI encoding by default, matching VB6 behavior. Characters above code point 255 are silently converted to `?`. Specifying `Encoding utf_8` on the **Open** statement extends this to support UTF-8 for UDT **String** members in **Binary** mode. Both the write and the read **Open** statement must name the same encoding:
>
> ```tb
> Open filename For Binary Access Write Encoding utf_8 As #n
> ' ... Put #n, , myRecord ...
> Close #n
>
> Open filename For Binary Access Read Encoding utf_8 As #n
> ' ... Get #n, , myRecord ...
> Close #n
> ```

## docs/Reference/Core/OrElse.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> When guarding against a **Nothing** object reference, **OrElse** is required---not **Or**. **Or** evaluates both operands unconditionally, so if the left operand is **True** (the object is **Nothing**), the right operand is still evaluated and dereferencing the **Nothing** object raises an "Object not set" error at runtime. The correct pattern is:
>
> ```tb
> If (obj Is Nothing) OrElse (obj.Member Is Nothing) Then
> ```
>
> Using **Or** in this situation compiles without error but fails at runtime.

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC rejects assignments to a property that has only a **Property Get** procedure (no **Property Let** or **Property Set**). The compiler raises an error: "Unable to bind to reference; this is a ReadOnly binder". VB6 silently accepted these assignments in some cases, so code ported from VB6 that writes to a get-only property will fail in twinBASIC. This was confirmed as intended behavior; a related error-reporting defect was fixed in BETA 307.
>
> A common source of this error in ported VB6 code is an implicit default member call --- an expression where VB6 silently resolved a write through a class's default property or method. twinBASIC requires explicit member access in these cases. Reviewing code for implicit default member usage is a recommended step when porting VB6 projects.

## docs/Reference/Core/Property.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1109102306965848084, 1352268312117252126, 1446528354307014871, 1483873341864411347, 1200568858218610830, 1236258934952558693]

> [!NOTE]
>
> In VBA and VB6, a **Property Get** and its paired **Property Let** must declare the same data type for the return value and the *value* parameter respectively; mismatched types are a compiler error. twinBASIC currently compiles such pairs without error or warning. Code that relies on mismatched **Property Get** / **Property Let** types will compile but may produce unexpected behavior if callers assume the two types match. A warning (or error) for this pattern is planned. One legitimate exception is certain Windows COM interfaces that define inconsistent Get/Let pairs by specification or that map most naturally to different VB types on each side; making this unconditionally an error would prevent valid COM interface implementations.

## docs/Reference/Core/Property.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1109102306965848084, 1246918643762204795, 1446528354307014871, 1483873341864411347, 1200568858218610830, 1236258934952558693]

> [!NOTE]
> When defining COM interfaces in twinBASIC, **Property Let** generates a `propput` attribute in the type library and allows assignment without the **Set** keyword at the call site. **Property Set** generates `propputref` and requires the **Set** keyword on assignment. For WinRT or external COM interfaces that use `[propput]` with object-typed parameters, **Property Let** is the correct twinBASIC translation --- not **Property Set**.
>
> The semantic distinction matters when the property type has a default member (for example `ADODB.Connection`): using **Property Let** (propput) invokes the default member of the assigned object rather than storing the object reference itself, whereas **Property Set** (propputref) stores the reference directly.

> [!NOTE]
> Generic classes parameterized with a type parameter `T` cannot provide a single property setter that covers both value types and object references. **Property Let** applies to value types; **Property Set** applies to object references. Because the author of a generic class does not know at write-time whether `T` will resolve to a value type or a reference type, satisfying the setter requirement requires writing both forms with a runtime guard, or restricting the type parameter's usage. A unified `Property Put` form was proposed as a language addition that the compiler would rewrite into the appropriate **Let** or **Set** at generic-close time, but this was not yet implemented as of early 2024.

## docs/Reference/Core/Property.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1109102306965848084, 1246918643762204795, 1352268312117252126, 1446528354307014871, 1483873341864411347, 1200568858218610830]

> [!NOTE]
> In a **Property Let** or **Property Set** declaration the assigned value must always be the final argument in the parameter list. Because VB/twinBASIC syntax also requires that no required argument follows an optional one, an optional index parameter cannot appear after the required value parameter. As a result, a property with an optional index cannot be expressed as a single property procedure --- the developer must either always pass the index explicitly or provide separate named accessor methods. A language-design discussion on allowing optional arguments at any position is tracked at https://github.com/twinbasic/lang-design/issues/58.

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC versions before BETA 980, **Put** and **Get** fail silently when a UDT contains a **String** member whose data is 65,536 bytes (64 KB) or larger. The two-byte length prefix used for variable-length strings overflows and wraps around, so the write or read appears to succeed but the data is truncated. This was fixed in BETA 980.

> A workaround for earlier versions is to replace the **String** member with a **Byte** array:
>
> ```tb
> Private Type tData
>     bData1() As Byte
> End Type
> ```
>
> This avoids the length-overflow and also removes the need to specify a UTF-8 encoding on the [**Open**](Open) statement.

## docs/Reference/Core/ReDim.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1112631246338662420, 1126698055547236443]

> [!NOTE]
> **ReDim** cannot be applied to a **Public** array member of a class from outside that class. The compiler automatically generates a **Property Get** for any public array field, and **Property Get** returns a copy of the array rather than a reference to the original storage. Applying **ReDim** to the copy raises TB5063 ("unrecognized symbol for array"); writing to an element of the copy (e.g. `obj.arr(0) = 1`) raises TB5001 ("cannot coerce type").

To resize an array held by another class, declare the field **Private** and expose a dedicated method:

```tb
' Inside the class:
Private arr() As Long

Public Sub ResizeArr(newSize As Long)
    ReDim arr(newSize)
End Sub
```

The fix is to add an explicit declaration before the first **ReDim** --- for example, `Dim D() As Integer` --- leaving the **ReDim** statement itself unchanged.

>
> - **Procedure level:** place `[ IgnoreWarnings(TB0016) ]` immediately before the `Sub` or `Function`.
> - **Module level:** place `[ IgnoreWarnings(TB0016) ]` immediately before the `Class` or `Module` declaration.
> - **Project-wide:** use the *Compiler warnings* section of the project Settings page.
>
> Project-wide suppression does not affect warnings originating in built-in packages --- those must be corrected in the package source itself.

## docs/Reference/Core/Return.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1064708394033881148]

> [!NOTE]

The **Exit Sub** / **Exit Function** / **Exit Property** forms remain available and coexist with **Return**.

> [!NOTE]
> In a `Case Is` clause, binary operators such as `And` and `Or` bind to the *operand* of the comparison, not to two comparison results. Writing `Case Is < 5 And lValue < 10` is parsed as `lValue < (5 And lValue < 10)` --- not as `(lValue < 5) And (lValue < 10)`. To combine two conditions in a single `Case` branch, use a nested `If` statement inside the branch, or restructure the `Select Case` to test each condition in separate `Case` clauses. In early twinBASIC builds this parsing produced an internal compiler error; it was corrected in BETA 209.

> [!NOTE]
> Assigning the same object variable to multiple array elements stores the same reference in each element. Mutations to the object are visible through every element that references it. To store independent objects, create a new instance before each assignment:
>
> ```tb
> Dim Personen(0 To 2) As clsPerson
> Dim i As Long
> For i = 0 To 2
>     Set Personen(i) = New clsPerson
>     Personen(i).Name = "Person " & (i + 1)
> Next i
> ```

## docs/Reference/Core/Set.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1086699374073085992, 1129918280237326486, 1352268312117252126, 1357341813098418257, 1504076759602040953, 1113586767321374730]

> [!NOTE]
> When a class has a `[DefaultMember]` method whose parameters are all optional, passing an instance of that class as an argument to `Array()` --- or in any simple data expression --- causes twinBASIC to evaluate the default member rather than treat the value as an object reference. This follows the MS-VBAL specification for default member evaluation. The result is that the array element contains the return value of the default member, not a reference to the object.
>
> Use explicit **Set** to assign object references into array elements:
>
> ```tb
> Dim arr(0 To 1) As MyClass
> Set arr(0) = obj1  ' stores a reference
> Set arr(1) = obj2  ' stores a reference
> ```
>
> Alternatively, use a `Collection` instead of an array --- collection elements always store references. Note that array-to-array copying (`arr2 = arr`) does not trigger default member evaluation and correctly preserves existing references.

## docs/Reference/Core/Set.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1086699374073085992, 1129918280237326486, 1314806984557596683, 1357341813098418257, 1504076759602040953, 1113586767321374730]

> [!NOTE]
> When **Set** assigns one interface-typed variable to another, the runtime calls `IUnknown::QueryInterface` internally to obtain the requested interface. Because `stdole.IUnknown` and `stdole.IDispatch` are marked as restricted COM interfaces, their methods --- including `QueryInterface`, `AddRef`, and `Release` --- cannot be called directly from code. To obtain an interface from an object, use `Set iFoo = obj` with both variables declared as their respective interface types; the runtime performs the `QueryInterface` call. To test whether an object supports an interface before assignment, use `If TypeOf obj Is IFoo Then Set foo = obj`. When working with raw pointers where **Set** is insufficient, define a non-restricted `IUnknown` in the project or reference an equivalent from an external library.

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC does not have a `Using`/`End Using` construct. In .NET languages, `Using` exists to guarantee cleanup in a garbage-collected environment where object lifetime is non-deterministic. twinBASIC, like VB6, uses reference-counting: an object is released as soon as the last reference to it is dropped. To release an object before the end of a procedure, `Set foo = Nothing` is sufficient.

## docs/Reference/Core/Sub.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053417989397024889, 1261260399161114727]

> [!NOTE]
> **Win64 compiled code size limit per procedure.** The Win64 compiler encodes branch offsets in 24 bits, which limits the assembled machine code for a single **Sub**, **Function**, or **Property** procedure to 16 MB (`&HFFFFFF`). Procedures that exceed this limit produce a "Compilation Unit Too Large" error during the code-generation phase.
>
> This constraint applies only to executable code inside the procedure body. Module-level declarations --- including large array declarations such as `Public Pattern(50000) As String` --- do not count toward the limit.
>
> The compiler settings labeled "increase to compile larger projects" (Project Settings > Compiler > Symbol Table) affect the symbol table, not the per-procedure code size, and will not resolve this error.
>
> The recommended fix is to split the oversized procedure into multiple smaller procedures. For example, a single procedure containing a large number of conditional initialization blocks can be split into groups (one per letter of the alphabet, or one per logical section). Win32 builds are not subject to the same encoding constraint and are less likely to hit the limit under equivalent conditions.
>
> This limit is a known architectural constraint that requires internal changes to the compiler before it can be raised.

_Source threads: 1099362561482301523 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-05-12 to 2023-05-15_
_Reviewer note: Consider adding an identical or summary note to docs/Reference/Core/Function.md and docs/Reference/Core/Property.md, since the limit applies equally to all three procedure kinds._

> [!NOTE]
> `#Const` declarations are private to the module in which they appear and cannot be made visible to other modules. There is no `#Public Const` equivalent. Project-wide conditional compilation constants must be defined in the project's compilation settings (Project Settings UI), not with `#Const`. A common pattern is to derive a module-local alias from a project-level setting: `#Const HasSha512 = (CRYPT_HAS_SHA512 <> 0)`, where `CRYPT_HAS_SHA512` is a project-defined compilation setting and `HasSha512` is the local constant used in `#If` expressions within that module.

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1436549533910962176, 1441409117288665171, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1505726092479041556, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1457034604769706168, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1449383679309905940, 1458435282809393248, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

> [!NOTE]
> Assigning between two `Private Type` variables that share the same name but are declared in different modules compiles and runs without error, even when the field layouts differ. The compiler treats such an assignment as a raw memory copy --- the same operation performed by [**LSet**](LSet). No type-mismatch error is raised. This matches VB6 behavior, and also applies when the same-named types come from two different external typelibs.
>
> This can be used to reinterpret the raw bits of a value as a different type --- for example, extracting an object pointer as a `Long` --- without calling `RtlMoveMemory`. The pattern requires two modules, each declaring a `Private Type` with the same name but different field types, with at least one padding field so that the total size exceeds 8 bytes:

```tb
' Module A
Private Type Caster
    Value As Long
    Pad   As Long
End Type

Function ObjectToLong(ByVal Obj As Object) As Long
    Dim src As CasterObj
    Dim dst As Caster
    src.Value = Obj
    dst = src          ' Raw memory copy between same-named Private Types.
    ObjectToLong = dst.Value
End Function
```

```tb
' Module B
Private Type Caster
    Value As Object
    Pad   As Long
End Type
```

> [!WARNING]
> Casting an `Object` to a `Long` this way increments the object's reference count, which will not be released automatically. Casting a `Long` back to an `Object` does not call `AddRef` on the source. Reference counts must be managed manually when using this pattern.

_Source threads: 1053405466409058335 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2022-12-16 to 2022-12-17_
_Reviewer note: The example code uses a second module type name `CasterObj` in module A but the type is declared as `Caster` in module B. The two modules must each declare `Private Type Caster` with those different field layouts. > [!NOTE]
> Any UDT field that holds a memory address or OS handle must be declared `As LongPtr`, not `As Long`. On a 32-bit target `LongPtr` is 4 bytes --- identical to `Long` --- so the code is source-compatible. On a 64-bit target `LongPtr` is 8 bytes; declaring such a field `As Long` silently truncates the high 32 bits of every pointer value and causes access violations at runtime. This applies to Win32 Types ported from VB6, such as `BITMAP` (`bmBits`), `LOGFONT` (not applicable), `POINTAPI`, and any custom struct that wraps an `HWND`, `HDC`, `HBITMAP`, or similar handle.

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053405466409058335, 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1441409117288665171, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1505726092479041556, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1457034604769706168, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1449383679309905940, 1458435282809393248, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, `Double` and `LongLong` fields inside a `Type` block are aligned at 8-byte boundaries in both 32-bit and 64-bit builds. VB6 uses a 4-byte packing alignment by default, so the same UDT can produce a different `LenB()` result and a different memory layout under each compiler. For example, a type containing a `Long`, a `Double`, and an `Integer` returns 16 bytes under VB6 but 24 bytes under 32-bit twinBASIC. Code that shares binary UDT data with VB6 ActiveX components, reads files written by VB6, or passes UDT pointers to APIs that were designed against VB6 layouts must add `[PackingAlignment(4)]` to the type to restore the 4-byte-aligned layout:
>
> ```tb
> [PackingAlignment(4)]
> Public Type MyUDT
>     ID   As Long
>     Cost As Double
>     Qty  As Integer
> End Type
> ```
>
> This is the same adjustment that C/C++ exposes as `#pragma pack(4)`. When translating C structures, check for a separate `#pragma pack` directive in an included header, because the effective alignment can differ from the structure's apparent field sizes.

_Source threads: 1436549533910962176 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-11-08 to 2025-11-10_
_Reviewer note: Verify that 32-bit twinBASIC does in fact give LenB = 24 for the Long+Double+Integer example cited in the thread, and that [PackingAlignment(4)] restores LenB = 16. The existing twinBASIC enhancements section already mentions [PackingAlignment] but only in a general sense; this note adds the specific VB6 compatibility context._

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053405466409058335, 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1436549533910962176, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1505726092479041556, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1457034604769706168, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1449383679309905940, 1458435282809393248, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

### Known limitations of lifecycle hooks

The following limitations apply to UDT lifecycle hooks (`Type_Initialize`, `Type_Terminate`, `Type_Assignment`, `Type_Conversion`) in the current release.

**`Type_Initialize` does not fire for module-level variables.** When a UDT that implements `Type_Initialize` is declared as a form-level or module-level variable, `Type_Initialize` is never called. `Type_Terminate` does fire when the module is torn down. Code that depends on `Type_Initialize` to set up internal state must handle the case where the hook may not have run.

> [!NOTE]
> This limitation does not affect local (procedure-level) variables, which receive `Type_Initialize` normally.

**Array element assignment calls `Type_Terminate` immediately after each write.** Assigning to an element of an array of UDTs that implement `Type_Terminate` causes `Type_Terminate` to fire on the element immediately after the assignment rather than when the array is freed. For example:

```tb
Dim StrArr(0 To 9) As HSTRING
For i = 0 To 9
    StrArr(i) = CStr(i)   ' Type_Terminate fires here on every iteration
Next i
' All elements now hold null/invalid state
```

This makes direct assignment to arrays of resource-managing UDTs unsafe. Prefer a helper Sub that takes a pointer or index parameter and updates the element without triggering a redundant `Type_Terminate`.

**`Property Let` always copies the RHS, even when declared `ByRef`.** The compiler makes an implicit copy of the caller's value before passing it to a property setter. As a result, `StrPtr` inside the setter differs from `StrPtr` of the caller's original variable. The same applies to `Type_Assignment` when called through a property-let setter. When zero-copy semantics are required, use a plain `Sub` (e.g. `SetValue`) or access the field directly instead of routing through a property.

Passing a string literal to a `ByRef String` parameter also creates a temporary copy, because string literals in the compiled binary are not real BSTRs.

**Returning a resource-managing UDT from a `Function` is unsafe.** When a UDT implements both `Type_Terminate` and `Type_Conversion`, the order in which they fire on the returned temporary is non-deterministic. In some runs `Type_Conversion` fires first (correct); in others `Type_Terminate` fires first, destroying the resource before the caller can read it, leading to an access-violation crash. The safe alternative is to pass the UDT `ByRef` as an output parameter of a `Sub`, where lifetime is fully under the caller's control.

**`[IgnoreWarnings(TB0018)]` has no effect inside a UDT body.** The attribute that suppresses implicit narrowing conversion warnings does not take effect when placed inside a `Type` definition. The warnings are still emitted. Apply the attribute at module level instead, or restructure the code to avoid the narrowing conversion.

_Source threads: 1441409117288665171 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-11-22 to 2025-12-01_

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053405466409058335, 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1436549533910962176, 1441409117288665171, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1457034604769706168, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1449383679309905940, 1458435282809393248, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

> [!IMPORTANT]
> When a **Type** (UDT) is used to interoperate with a C API whose parameter is a C `union`, the UDT must reserve memory for the *entire* union, not only the first member. If only the first member is declared (for example, `Type sfEvent : Type As Long : End Type`) and the DLL writes data to the full union extent, the DLL overwrites memory beyond the UDT's allocation and corrupts the call stack. Include a byte-array padding member sized to the largest union variant:
>
> ```tb
> Type sfEvent
>     Type As sfEventType
>     Data(0 To 31) As Byte   ' reserves the full 32-byte union extent
> End Type
> ```

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053405466409058335, 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1436549533910962176, 1441409117288665171, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1505726092479041556, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1449383679309905940, 1458435282809393248, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

### Known limitations

**`Type_Terminate` fires before the return value is usable.** When a UDT that defines a `Type_Terminate` member is used as the return type of a function, the destructor runs before the caller can read the returned value. Any cleanup performed in `Type_Terminate` --- such as releasing a pointer or handle held by the UDT --- therefore destroys the resource prematurely. As a workaround, avoid returning such UDTs directly from functions; instead, pass an output parameter `ByRef` or return a handle/index that the caller resolves separately.

**Calling a method on an array element causes an Access Violation.** Invoking a member procedure directly through an array subscript --- for example, `MyArr(i).MethodName` --- produces an Access Violation at run time. Copy the element to a local variable first, call the method on the variable, and copy it back if the UDT was modified:

```tb
Dim temp As MyUDT
temp = MyArr(i)
temp.MethodName
MyArr(i) = temp
```

> Sub Example(Optional ByVal pData As Long = 0)

>     Dim data As MyType

> End Sub
> ```
>

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053405466409058335, 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1436549533910962176, 1441409117288665171, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1505726092479041556, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1457034604769706168, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1458435282809393248, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

> [!NOTE]
> A `Type` that contains a **Variant** field (or any other non-simple field) cannot be passed `ByVal` to a procedure. If two overloaded procedures accept different UDT types `ByVal`, and one of those UDTs defines a `Type_Assignment` sub that accepts a **Variant**, the compiler cannot disambiguate the overloads --- any value can be coerced into the **Variant**-accepting UDT through `Type_Assignment`, producing an ambiguity error even when the caller passes a clearly typed argument. Declare UDT parameters `ByRef` instead of `ByVal` when the UDT contains non-simple fields; `ByRef` prevents the coercion path and makes overloads unambiguous.

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1053405466409058335, 1071686119554568255, 1079323729613557801, 1096855154617241641, 1110672289848103023, 1232420328852947096, 1436549533910962176, 1441409117288665171, 1441848799554310205, 1443537199579660420, 1450087715545813024, 1470627964558245930, 1505726092479041556, 1096135375900127363, 1327014988128456704, 1457034604769706168, 1223378818807369808, 1285153775069429840, 1440638912195334196, 1449383679309905940, 1485648451479015544, 1488678693046845613]

> [!NOTE]
> Under the Microsoft x64 calling convention, **ByVal** UDT arguments do not always produce a true by-value copy. Only UDTs whose total size is exactly 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes are passed in a register as a true value. UDTs of size 3, 5, 6, or 7 bytes, or larger than 8 bytes, are automatically passed by reference (a pointer to a caller-allocated copy) even when the parameter is declared **ByVal** --- the bytes are not padded to the next power of two. A single-member UDT whose member is a standard-width intrinsic type (e.g. one **Long**, one **LongPtr**) is equivalent to declaring that intrinsic type directly for the purposes of interop.

## docs/Reference/Core/Type.md · example

### Example -- wrapping a WinRT HSTRING handle

The following pattern, confirmed by WaynePhillipsEA, shows how to implement a UDT that wraps the WinRT `HSTRING` opaque handle type. Key points:

- `Type_Assignment(RHS As String)` uses `WindowsDeleteString` to release any existing handle, then `WindowsCreateStringReference` via a helper (`StrRef`) to obtain a fast-pass reference --- only safe when the HSTRING lifetime does not outlive the caller's string variable (argument-passing).
- `SetValue` uses `WindowsCreateString` for full ownership copy --- use this when assigning from a local variable where the caller's string may go out of scope.
- `Type_Assignment(ByVal RHS As LongPtr)` allows assigning a raw HSTRING handle directly.
- `Type_Conversion` reconstructs a `String` by reading the raw buffer via `WindowsGetStringRawBuffer` and writing it directly into the return variable with `SysReAllocString`.
- `Type_Terminate` releases the handle with `WindowsDeleteString`.

```tb
Public Type HSTRING
    Ptr As LongPtr

    Private Sub Type_Assignment(RHS As String)
        WindowsDeleteString Me.Ptr
        Me.Ptr = StrRef(RHS)   ' fast-pass reference -- safe for argument passing only
    End Sub

    Private Sub Type_Assignment(ByVal RHS As LongPtr)
        WindowsDeleteString Me.Ptr
        Me.Ptr = RHS
    End Sub

    Private Function Type_Conversion() As String
        SysReAllocString VarPtr(Type_Conversion), WindowsGetStringRawBuffer(Me.Ptr)
    End Function

    Private Sub Type_Terminate()
        WindowsDeleteString Me.Ptr
    End Sub

    Sub SetValue(sValue As String)
        WindowsDeleteString Me.Ptr
        WindowsCreateString StrPtr(sValue), Len(sValue), Me.Ptr
    End Sub
End Type
```

> [!NOTE]
> Because `Property Let` always copies the RHS (see [Known limitations](#known-limitations-of-lifecycle-hooks)), routing `Type_Assignment` through a property setter produces a copy rather than a reference. When zero-copy argument passing is required, pass the `HSTRING` variable `ByRef` directly.

To diagnose use-after-free bugs in UDTs that manage raw memory, enable the **Immediate Memory Invalidation** project setting. When active, freed memory is immediately overwritten with a recognisable pattern (visible as exclamation marks when interpreted as string data), making dangling-pointer reads immediately apparent at runtime rather than causing silent corruption.

## docs/Reference/CustomControls/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1108346874768936960, 1304943281721053266]

> [!NOTE]
> Prior to twinBASIC BETA 229, all controls in this package failed to repaint when their host form was resized. The affected controls became invisible until the mouse moved over them. This was a known bug, confirmed and fixed in BETA 229. Built-in VB controls on the same form were not affected.
>
> For projects targeting an earlier build, the following workaround forces a repaint after the resize gesture ends. Because `RedrawWindow` called directly inside the `Resize` event has no effect, the repaint must be deferred until after the handler returns. A timer-based debounce also avoids repeated redraws while the user is dragging the window border.

```tb
' Module-level state
Private mItv As Long

' Declare RedrawWindow in your form or module
Private Declare PtrSafe Function RedrawWindow Lib "user32" _
    (ByVal hWnd As LongPtr, ByVal lprcUpdate As LongPtr, _
     ByVal hrgnUpdate As LongPtr, ByVal flags As Long) As Long

Private Const RDW_INVALIDATE  As Long = &H1
Private Const RDW_ERASE       As Long = &H4
Private Const RDW_ALLCHILDREN As Long = &H80
Private Const RDW_UPDATENOW   As Long = &H100

Private Sub Form_Resize()
    mItv = 0
    Timer1.Enabled = True
End Sub

Private Sub Timer1_Timer()
    mItv = mItv + 1
    If mItv >= 3 Then
        Timer1.Enabled = False
        RedrawWindow hwnd, 0, 0, RDW_UPDATENOW Or RDW_INVALIDATE Or RDW_ERASE Or RDW_ALLCHILDREN
    End If
End Sub
```

Set `Timer1.Interval` to 100. The timer fires three times (~300 ms of no resize activity) before calling `RedrawWindow`, ensuring the repaint occurs after the user has stopped dragging.

## docs/Reference/CustomControls/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1062707297706586123, 1304943281721053266]

> [!NOTE]
> Lightweight controls do not implement mouse capture. When a mouse button is pressed inside a control and the cursor is then moved outside its bounds while the button remains held, **MouseMove** stops firing. Standard Win32 behavior would keep the control receiving mouse move events until the button is released. A workaround is to call the Win32 `SetCapture` API on the parent form's window handle in the `MouseDown` handler, track the pressed state with a flag, and forward the resulting `WM_MOUSEMOVE` messages to the control manually until `MouseUp` is received.

## docs/Reference/Data-Types.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1054031803087851530, 1357009211179139200, 1442172881596584078, 1148996503675879474, 1260984179051728956, 1449211458683408515, 1460777854714515728]

> [!NOTE]
> An unsuffixed hex literal in the range `&H8000` through `&HFFFF` is typed as **Integer**, not **Long**. When the value is used in a **Long** context --- for example, OR-ed into a Win32 style bitmask --- the runtime sign-extends it to `&HFFFFxxxx`, producing a large negative **Long** instead of the intended positive value. The fix is to append the Long type suffix: write `&H8000&` instead of `&H8000`. The compiler does not currently warn about this widening. A common symptom is a Win32 API call (such as `CreateWindowEx`) failing with an unexpected error when a constant in this range is included in the style argument.

> [!NOTE]
> Assigning a **LongPtr** array to a function declared to return **Long()** produces no IDE warning and no compile-time error. In a 64-bit build, **LongPtr** is 8 bytes and **Long** is always 4 bytes, so the assignment silently truncates any value whose magnitude exceeds 2,147,483,647. The IDE hover tooltip over a **LongPtr** variable may also show the resolved concrete type (**Long** or **LongLong**) rather than **LongPtr** itself. ## docs/Reference/Glossary.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> A line that starts with a comment (`'` or `Rem`) placed immediately after a line ending with `_` **ends** the continued statement at the `_`, not at the comment. The comment and any following lines are treated as separate statements. For example:
>
> ```tb
> MsgBox "foo" _
> ' this comment ends the continuation
> MsgBox "bar"   ' parsed as a second, separate call
> ```
>
> This behavior matches VBx (VB6 and VBA) and is retained for backward compatibility. To comment out an alternate continuation line during development, use the block comment syntax (`/* ... */`) or conditional compilation (`#If`/`#Else`/`#End If`).

## docs/Reference/Operators.md · new-section

## Dictionary Access

- `!` -- accesses a field or key on an object by passing the following identifier as a string to the object's default member; equivalent to calling the default member with a string argument

The syntax `object!identifier` is shorthand for `object("identifier")`. It is most commonly used with Recordsets and Collection-like objects:

```tb
Dim rs As ADODB.Recordset
Debug.Print rs!CustomerName   ' equivalent to rs("CustomerName")
```

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, the token immediately after `!` must be a plain identifier. A known parser bug (issue #1450) causes the compile to fail when that token matches a reserved keyword --- for example, `rs!Width` and `rs!Error` both trigger a parse error because `Width` and `Error` are recognized as keywords rather than field names. The workaround is to enclose the name in square brackets: `rs![Width]`, `rs![Error]`.

## docs/Reference/VB/App/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1250428295707627550, 1271657049419415604, 1352268312117252126, 1401751417064259594, 1443578964743422053, 1450170203714490439, 1354707710503026708, 1403137481641037914, 1412397033641214053, 1443849085286088924, 1225926859133550603]

> [!NOTE]
> **App.Path** returns the IDE executable's folder when the project has not yet been saved to disk. Once the project is saved, **App.Path** returns the project folder while running from the IDE, and the EXE folder when running as a compiled executable. This matches VB6 behaviour: VB6 also pointed **App.Path** at the VB6.EXE folder in the same situation.

> [!NOTE]
> When a compiled executable is launched through the IDE's post-build launch link, the Win32 `GetCurrentDirectoryW` API returns the System32 directory rather than the executable's folder. Running the same executable directly from Windows Explorer returns the executable's directory. This is a Win32 process-launch behaviour difference and not a compiler bug. Applications that depend on the current directory matching the executable location should call `SetCurrentDirectory` with **App.Path** at startup.

### IsInIDE and Form Preview mode

`App.IsInIDE` returns **True** both during a normal IDE run and during Form Preview. Form Preview is a separate execution context: only that form's `Form_Load` fires --- the project's startup object and `Sub Main` do not execute. There is no `App.IsInPreview` or equivalent property to distinguish a Form Preview run from a full IDE run.

## docs/Reference/VB/App/index.md · example

### Loading resources from the last compiled build when running from the IDE

Some Windows APIs load binary resources from an `HMODULE` --- for example, `IUIRibbonFramework.LoadUI` for the Windows Ribbon Framework. The module handle from `GetModuleHandleW()` is only valid for a compiled executable, not when the project runs inside the IDE.

The pattern below detects IDE execution using `Debug.Assert` and, when in the IDE, loads the most recently compiled `.exe` as a data-only module so the resources are available:

```tb
Private hLastExe As LongPtr

Private Function MakeTrue(ByRef x As Boolean) As Boolean
    x = True: MakeTrue = True
End Function

Private Sub Form_Load() Handles Form.Load
    Dim InIde As Boolean: Debug.Assert MakeTrue(InIde)
    If InIde Then
        If (App.LastBuildPath = "") Or (PathFileExists(App.LastBuildPath) = 0) Then
            MsgBox "To run from the IDE, build the project first.", _
                   vbCritical Or vbOKOnly, App.Title
            Unload Me
            Exit Sub
        End If
        hLastExe = LoadLibraryExW(StrPtr(App.LastBuildPath), 0, _
                                   LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE Or LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_IMAGE_RESOURCE)
        pFramework.LoadUI hLastExe, StrPtr("APPLICATION_RIBBON")
    Else
        pFramework.LoadUI GetModuleHandleW(), StrPtr("APPLICATION_RIBBON")
    End If
End Sub

Private Sub Form_Unload(Cancel As Integer) Handles Form.Unload
    If hLastExe <> 0 Then FreeLibrary hLastExe
End Sub
```

`Debug.Assert MakeTrue(InIde)` sets `InIde` to `True` only inside the IDE, because the IDE's debug evaluator executes the `Assert` argument while a compiled build skips it. `App.LastBuildPath` is empty when the IDE has not yet produced a build in the current session, so the guard at the top of the `If InIde` block prevents a load attempt against a missing file.

## docs/Reference/VB/CheckBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1224653429121482784, 1226792632286707712, 1254784342513811527, 1330132086249754693, 1371232551070597160, 1417086895921561640, 1433364130257178906]

## Dark mode

The standard Win32 checkbox does not support dark mode through the [**BackColor**](#backcolor) and [**ForeColor**](#forecolor) properties alone. A partial dark appearance can be achieved by calling the `SetWindowTheme` API with the `"DarkMode_Explorer"` theme string:

```tb
Private Declare PtrSafe Function SetWindowTheme Lib "uxtheme.dll" ( _
    ByVal hwnd As LongPtr, _
    ByVal pszSubAppName As LongPtr, _
    ByVal pszSubIdList As LongPtr) As Long

' In Form_Load or after the control is created:
SetWindowTheme Check1.hWnd, StrPtr("DarkMode_Explorer"), 0
```

This darkens the box background, border, and checkmark. It does not change the caption text color, because `uxtheme.dll` provides no mechanism to override the foreground color for `BP_CHECKBOX` parts through the theme system.

> [!NOTE]
> To force a custom text color alongside the dark theme, the approach used in production applications (such as XYplorer) is IAT (Import Address Table) hooking: intercept the `DrawThemeText` and `DrawThemeTextEx` imports on `COMCTL32.DLL`, detect calls where `iPartId` equals `BP_RADIOBUTTON` or `BP_CHECKBOX`, and call `DrawThemeTextEx` with a `DTTOPTS` struct that sets the `DTT_TEXTCOLOR` flag and the target color. This preserves the built-in Windows 11 hover and click animations that would be lost with a fully custom-drawn control. The same technique applies to [**OptionButton**](../OptionButton).

As of October 2025, there is no built-in dark mode property on the standard VB controls. Support for automatic dark mode is on the roadmap but is not expected before the twinBASIC v1 release. The [CustomControls package](../../CustomControls/CustomControls Package) controls offer fuller visual customization in the meantime.

## docs/Reference/VB/Clipboard/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1165019755237879908, 1441092753084911636, 1394331563503915008, 1356328745044283564, 1125359845936205844]

To place a bitmap handle onto the clipboard without `SetData`, use the Win32 clipboard API directly:

```tb
Declare Function OpenClipboard Lib "user32" (ByVal hWndNewOwner As LongPtr) As Long
Declare Function EmptyClipboard Lib "user32" () As Long
Declare Function SetClipboardData Lib "user32" (ByVal uFormat As Long, ByVal hMem As LongPtr) As LongPtr
Declare Function CloseClipboard Lib "user32" () As Long

Const CF_BITMAP As Long = 2

Sub CopyBitmapToClipboard(ByVal hBmp As LongPtr)
    OpenClipboard 0
    EmptyClipboard
    SetClipboardData CF_BITMAP, hBmp
    CloseClipboard
End Sub
```

## docs/Reference/VB/ComboBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1128963066055368794, 1243201385734996009, 1361065359620309113, 1385247357800550474, 1339539666046550076, 1362056785804136540, 1422908698275217428, 1425862549919764592, 1445526310116917463]

> [!NOTE]
>
> **`CB_SETMINVISIBLE` and drop-down item count before Beta 809.** In twinBASIC prior to Beta 809, sending the Windows API message `CB_SETMINVISIBLE` via `SendMessage` to control the number of visible rows in the drop-down list added 8 to the requested value, so the drop-down displayed more items than requested. Additionally, each successive opening of the drop-down by clicking its button increased the visible row count by 8 even without the API call. Combo1.AddItem "Apple"
```tb
Combo1.ItemData(Combo1.NewIndex) = 101

Combo1.AddItem "Banana"
Combo1.ItemData(Combo1.NewIndex) = 102

Dim id As LongPtr
id = Combo1.ItemData(Combo1.ListIndex)
```

## docs/Reference/VB/ComboBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1128963066055368794, 1243201385734996009, 1361065359620309113, 1382076722236883045, 1385247357800550474, 1339539666046550076, 1362056785804136540, 1422908698275217428, 1445526310116917463]

## Dark mode

Applying a dark appearance to a **ComboBox** requires two separate `SetWindowTheme` calls because the control has two distinct child windows: the edit/button portion and the drop-down list.

```tb
Private Declare PtrSafe Function SetWindowTheme Lib "uxtheme.dll" ( _
    ByVal hwnd As LongPtr, _
    ByVal pszSubAppName As LongPtr, _
    ByVal pszSubIdList As LongPtr) As Long

Private Type COMBOBOXINFO
    cbSize      As Long
    rcItem      As RECT
    rcButton    As RECT
    stateButton As Long
    hwndCombo   As LongPtr
    hwndItem    As LongPtr
    hwndList    As LongPtr
End Type

Private Declare PtrSafe Function GetComboBoxInfo Lib "user32.dll" ( _
    ByVal hwndCombo As LongPtr, _
    ByRef pcbi As COMBOBOXINFO) As Long

Private Sub ApplyDarkMode()
    ' Style the edit and button portion
    SetWindowTheme Combo1.hWnd, StrPtr("DarkMode_CFD"), 0

    ' Style the drop-down list and its scrollbar
    Dim cbi As COMBOBOXINFO
    cbi.cbSize = LenB(cbi)
    GetComboBoxInfo Combo1.hWnd, cbi
    SetWindowTheme cbi.hwndList, StrPtr("DarkMode_Explorer"), 0

    ' Set colors to match
    Combo1.BackColor = RGB(32, 32, 32)
    Combo1.ForeColor = RGB(240, 240, 240)
End Sub
```

`"DarkMode_CFD"` styles the edit field and drop-down button; `"DarkMode_Explorer"` styles the drop-down list and its scrollbar. Applying `"DarkMode_CFD"` alone to the combo `hWnd` is not sufficient to darken the list.

> [!NOTE]
> Prior to BETA 890, twinBASIC had a bug where the drop-down list background was drawn unconditionally using `GetSysColorBrush(COLOR_WINDOW)`, overriding `BackColor`. This was fixed in BETA 890, so `BackColor` and `ForeColor` now behave as in VB6.

> [!NOTE]
> The COM default member (dispatch ID 0) on **CommandButton** is the hidden `_Default` member, not **Value**. This matches VB6 and COM behavior: `_Default` and **Value** are separate members, and `_Default` carries `VB_VarUserMemId = 0`. In practice the two behave identically for most uses, but reflection code or late-bound dispatch code that reads dispatch ID 0 will resolve to `_Default`. **Value** was added in an early twinBASIC build after the initial release and is present in all current builds.

## docs/Reference/VB/CommandButton/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052545719887732746, 1052545719887732746, 1057604110247014481, 1125489357197938709, 1236711686031937547, 1283597985015529494, 1392106770263965766, 1323418341658071061, 1413428727072948277]

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, Visual Styles are enabled by default. When Visual Styles are active, Windows hides keyboard-shortcut underlines by default --- they are only revealed when the user presses the **Alt** key, which is standard native Windows behavior. VB6 displayed shortcut underlines permanently on buttons regardless of Visual Styles. To restore the VB6 appearance, send `WM_UPDATEUISTATE` from `Form_Load`:
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub Form_Load()
>     ' UIS_CLEAR = 2, UISF_HIDEACCEL = 2 (HIWORD of wParam)
>     PostMessageW hWnd, WM_UPDATEUISTATE, 2 + 2 * 65536, 0&
> End Sub
> ```
>
> This places `UIS_CLEAR` in the LOWORD and `UISF_HIDEACCEL` in the HIWORD of *wParam*, clearing the "hide accelerator" state for the form and its children.

## docs/Reference/VB/Data/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1449892975822770381, 1293277481452834888, 1323059625360097340, 1374771756124078170, 1401925246885560340]

> [!NOTE]
> **vbUseACE and project bitness.** The ACE database engine is a COM server that is installed per-bitness: a 32-bit twinBASIC project requires the 32-bit ACE engine (typically installed with 32-bit Microsoft Access or the 32-bit Access Database Engine redistributable), and a 64-bit project requires the 64-bit variant. When the bitnesses do not match, the engine's CLSID (`CD7791B9-43FD-42C5-AE42-8DD2811F0419`) is absent from the registry for the running process, and the Data control raises a COM error --- HRESULT `0x80040154` (class not registered) --- when attempting to connect. Switch the project's target bitness using the toolbar selector in the twinBASIC IDE to match the installed engine.

> [!NOTE]
> **vbUseACE navigation crash in 64-bit builds.** In 64-bit twinBASIC projects, clicking the transport (navigation) buttons on a Data control configured with **vbUseACE** can cause a native exception. The 32-bit configuration is not affected. Until this is resolved, projects that require record navigation with `.accdb` files should target 32-bit. As an alternative, the database can be saved or converted to `.mdb` format and [**DefaultType**](#defaulttype) set to **vbUseJet**; the Jet engine does not support the Access 2007+ file format but avoids the crash. Note that `.mdb` lacks features introduced in Access 2007 (larger row sizes, multi-value fields, attachments, and others).

_Source threads: 1215043920774565969 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-10-11 to 2024-10-31_

## docs/Reference/VB/Data/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1215043920774565969, 1449892975822770381, 1323059625360097340, 1374771756124078170, 1401925246885560340]

> [!NOTE]
> When [**DefaultType**](#defaulttype) is **vbUseODBC**, twinBASIC's runtime requires `MSRDO20.dll` (Remote Data Objects). This DLL is not installed on Windows 10 or Windows 11 by default; it is present only on machines that have VB6 installed. Copying `MSRDO20.dll` from a VB6 installation into `C:\Windows\SysWOW64` and registering it with `regsvr32` resolves the missing-DLL error, though further ODBC configuration may be needed depending on the connection string.
>
> When [**DefaultType**](#defaulttype) is **vbUseACE** and the database is an Access 2007+ `.accdb` file, twinBASIC requires the 32-bit Microsoft Access Database Engine (ACE) redistributable. Without it, opening an `.accdb` file raises a "Class not registered" error. Older `.mdb` files open correctly with **vbUseJet** and do not require the ACE redistributable.

## docs/Reference/VB/Data/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1215043920774565969, 1449892975822770381, 1293277481452834888, 1374771756124078170, 1401925246885560340]

> [!NOTE]
> Setting **DefaultType** to **vbUseODBC** on a Win64 build causes the control to fail at initialisation. The `Data.twin` initialisation code checks for **vbUseACE** first; when that check does not match, it falls through to the DAO path. DAO is a 32-bit-only library and cannot be loaded in a 64-bit process. There is currently no supported workaround within the **Data** control itself; the implementation requires a platform guard in `Data.twin` to handle the ODBC case on 64-bit. ACE does not support ODBCDirect, so a full fix may require a separate ADO-backed control for the Win64 ODBC use case.

> [!NOTE]
> When automating Microsoft Access from a standalone twinBASIC EXE, `DoCmd` and other Access object-model members (such as `DoCmd.SetWarnings` or `DoCmd.RunSQL`) require the database to be loaded through the Access application object. Opening a database with `DAO.OpenDatabase` does not create an Access application instance, so Access does not consider any database current and `DoCmd` calls will fail. To use the Access object model, open the database with `Access.OpenCurrentDatabase(path)` and obtain the DAO reference via `Access.CurrentDb`. To avoid the Access object model entirely, execute SQL directly on the DAO database object.

## docs/Reference/VB/Data/index.md · example

### Verifying ACE DAO registration independently of the Data control

The following declarations let a project verify that the ACE DAO engine is correctly registered for its current bitness without going through the Data control. If `New DAODBEngineACE` succeeds and `Version` returns a string such as `"16"`, the engine is registered correctly. If it raises "class not registered", the project bitness does not match the installed engine bitness, or the engine is not installed at all.

```tb
[CoClassId("CD7791B9-43FD-42C5-AE42-8DD2811F0419")]
CoClass DAODBEngineACE
    [Default] Interface IDAODBEngine
End CoClass

[InterfaceId("00000021-0000-0010-8000-00AA006D2EA4")]
Interface IDAODBEngine Extends stdole.IDispatch
    [DispId(10)] Property Get Properties() As stdole.IUnknown
    [DispId(&H60030000)] Property Get Version() As String
End Interface
```

Call it at run time to confirm the engine version:

> [!NOTE]
> Accessing any member of a form that has been unloaded---such as reading or writing a property or referencing a child control---causes the runtime to create a new instance of the form. This new instance is invisible and not shown to the user. Because the process cannot terminate while loaded forms exist, this invisible instance prevents the application from exiting. A common trigger is a loop that calls [**DoEvents**](../../../Modules/Interaction/DoEvents): if the user closes the form while **DoEvents** is processing, the loop must check that the form is still loaded before touching any of its members. This behavior is consistent with VB6 and is a consequence of the predeclared form object model.

> [!NOTE]
> **StartUpPosition** is applied to the window after **Form_Load** completes. Any Win32 `SetWindowPos` API call made inside **Form_Load** to position the window is overridden by the **StartUpPosition** setting, and the form ends up at the position determined by **StartUpPosition**. To control the window position manually, either set **StartUpPosition** to **vbStartUpManual** at design time, or defer the `SetWindowPos` call to after the form is fully shown (for example, in **Form_Activate** or via a **Timer**).

> [!NOTE]
> The IDE Form Preview runs the form's actual event code, including **QueryUnload**. If `Cancel` is set to non-zero inside **QueryUnload** --- for example, to confirm before closing --- the preview window's close button becomes non-functional, leaving the preview stuck. A workaround is to also call `Me.Close` (or `Me.Hide`) programmatically alongside the cancel, so the form unloads even when the OS-level close is intercepted.
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub Form_QueryUnload(Cancel As Integer, UnloadMode As Integer)
>     If MsgBox("Quit?", vbYesNo) = vbNo Then
>         Cancel = 1
>     End If
> End Sub
> ```
>
> In the form above, clicking the preview window's X button and choosing *No* leaves the preview open with no way to close it short of restarting the IDE.

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, the `Y` parameter of **MouseDown** and **MouseUp** event handlers must be declared as `OLE_YPOS_PIXELS`, not `Single`. VB6 silently coerced event-handler argument types to match the declared signature, so `Single` worked there. twinBASIC does not implement this implicit coercion: declaring `y As Single` produces error TB5018 ("unable to match this handler to its event member"). The correct signatures are:
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub Form_MouseDown(ByVal Button As Integer, ByVal Shift As Integer, ByVal x As Single, ByVal y As OLE_YPOS_PIXELS)
> Private Sub Form_MouseUp(ByVal Button As Integer, ByVal Shift As Integer, ByVal x As Single, ByVal y As OLE_YPOS_PIXELS)
> ```
>
> This requirement applies to any control that exposes **MouseDown** or **MouseUp** events, not only to **Form**.

>
> ```tb

> [!NOTE]
> Naming a property or method `Default` on a form class causes a **FormDesignerId mismatch** error at run time. The name conflicts with the compiler's reserved `Default` keyword. In twinBASIC, the same pattern causes the **QueryUnload** message box to appear a second time instead. Conversely, setting `Cancel = 1` (the cancel branch) exits the application rather than leaving the form open. This is a known VB6 compatibility gap, likely to be addressed in the forms overhaul.

> [!NOTE]
> Anchor constraints on controls are not applied at design time. This is by design: applying anchors while editing a form would make it very difficult to reposition or resize controls, because any designer resize would immediately trigger the anchor logic. Anchors take effect only at runtime.

> [!NOTE]
> When a project with anchored controls is run inside the twinBASIC IDE and the form is resized during that run, the anchor state is retained between runs. On the next run---without restarting the IDE---controls resize abnormally due to this stale state. If the form is not resized during a run the problem does not occur. The workaround is to restart the twinBASIC IDE after any run in which the form was resized. (Known IDE-level bug as of BETA 630.)

> [!NOTE]
> When **StartUpPosition** is **vbStartUpScreen** (center screen), twinBASIC repositions the window after [**Load**](#load) returns, discarding any [**Top**](#top) or [**Left**](#left) assignments made inside that event. To position a form programmatically from **Form_Load**, set **StartUpPosition** to **vbStartUpManual** at design time. This applies both to `Me.Top` / `Me.Left` inside the form's own **Load** handler and to assignments made via a named reference from another form (e.g. `frmFluxDisplay.Top = ...`).
>
> VB6 behaves the same way. However, earlier versions of twinBASIC's VB6 importer incorrectly defaulted imported forms to **vbStartUpScreen** rather than the VB6 default of **vbStartUpWindowsDefault**; this was acknowledged as a regression. If a VB6 project's programmatic positioning stops working after import, check that **StartUpPosition** has not been changed from its original VB6 value.

> [!NOTE]
> The **MinWidth**, **MinHeight**, **MaxWidth**, and **MaxHeight** properties had a confirmed designer bug in builds around beta 675 where the stored values were read back using the wrong scale mode (twips interpreted as pixels), causing the values to grow by a factor of approximately 15 on each project reload. The inflated dimensions caused the designer to attempt to render an impossibly large bitmap, making the form appear corrupted or invisible. The recommended workaround is to leave all four properties at their default value of `0` and enforce minimum or maximum window dimensions at runtime by subclassing the form window and handling the `WM_GETMINMAXINFO` message.

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC forms, **UserControl**s, **PictureBox**es, and **Frame**s are Unicode windows. When a Win32 common control is created with a twinBASIC container as its parent using `CreateWindowEx`, the container responds to the control's `WM_NOTIFYFORMAT` query with `NFR_UNICODE`. As a result, all subsequent `WM_NOTIFY` messages from that control use Unicode structures (for example, `TVN_ITEMEXPANDINGW` rather than `TVN_ITEMEXPANDINGA`). Code migrated from VB6 that handles `WM_NOTIFY` via subclassing and expects ANSI notification codes will silently miss events or read incorrect data.
>
> A project setting named **Use Unicode Common Control Notifications** (added in BETA 832) can revert the response to `NFR_ANSI` for manually created third-party controls. Projects that do not subclass `WM_NOTIFY` are unaffected.

VB6 exhibits the same ambiguity. The workaround is to rename the conflicting property.

> [!NOTE]
> **Cls** raises [**Paint**](#paint) after clearing in twinBASIC. In VB6, calling `Me.Cls` cleared the drawing surface without raising **Form_Paint**. In twinBASIC (prior to BETA 981), calling **Cls** fires **Paint** after clearing. Code that calls **Cls** from inside a **Paint** or repaint routine can therefore enter infinite recursion --- each clear immediately triggers another paint. From BETA 981 onward the behaviour matches VB6. Projects running earlier builds should guard against this by checking a flag before calling **Cls** from within **Paint**.

> [!NOTE]
> Showing a non-modal form from code running inside an ActiveX DLL or ActiveX Control raises run-time error 406: "Non-Modal forms cannot be displayed in this host application from an ActiveX DLL, ActiveX Control or property page." VB6 permitted this in certain hosting scenarios. This is a known open issue.

> [!NOTE]
> In VB6, calling **Move** to reposition a form fires a single **Resize** event that reflects all four property changes at once. In twinBASIC, the runtime fires a separate **Resize** event for each property that changes, so a call that updates all four coordinates can raise up to four consecutive **Resize** events. Code in `Form_Resize` that performs expensive recalculation or layout work will run multiple times unnecessarily. A guard variable set before the first resize handler completes can coalesce the duplicate calls until this behaviour is corrected by the runtime.
