> [!NOTE]
> In VB6, disabling the **MinButton** or **MaxButton** also removes the corresponding command from the title-bar system (context) menu. In twinBASIC the system menu commands remain enabled regardless of whether the button is present. To remove the commands, call the Win32 API in `Form_Load`:
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub Form_Load()
>     ' Remove the Minimize command from the system menu.
>     SetWindowLong hWnd, GWL_STYLE, _
>         (GetWindowLong(hWnd, GWL_STYLE)) And Not WS_MINIMIZEBOX
>     DeleteMenu GetSystemMenu(hWnd, False), SC_MINIMIZE, MF_BYCOMMAND
> End Sub
> ```
>
> Repeat with `SC_MAXIMIZE` and `WS_MAXIMIZEBOX` to remove the Maximize command. `GetSystemMenu`, `DeleteMenu`, `GetWindowLong`, `SetWindowLong`, and the required constants must be declared in the project (or imported from the Win32 API type library).

> [!NOTE]
> In a 64-bit twinBASIC project, **hWnd** returns a **LongLong** (as **LongPtr** resolves to **LongLong** on 64-bit). All Win32 User32 and GDI handles are guaranteed to fit in 32 bits, so narrowing to **Long** is safe for passing to third-party ActiveX controls or Win32 APIs that declare their handle parameters as **Long** (the classic `OLE_HANDLE` type). Plain `CLng()` is unsafe when the lower 32 bits have the high bit set (bit 31 / `&H80000000`), because **CLng** interprets that as a negative number and raises an overflow error. The safe narrowing pattern is:
>
> ```tb
> Function CLngTrunc(ByVal value As LongLong) As Long
>     GetMem4(VarPtr(value), CLngTrunc)
> End Function
> ```
>
> This reads the low four bytes of the handle directly, without sign extension.

_Source threads: 1440400793663574167 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-11-18_
_Reviewer note: Note targets the hWnd property subsection of Form/index.md. The same pattern applies to hDC and any other LongPtr handle property. Reviewer may wish to add a cross-reference to hDC or place the note at module level rather than under hWnd alone._

> [!WARNING]
> When handling `WM_CTLCOLORSTATIC`, `WM_CTLCOLOREDIT`, or any `WM_CTLCOLOR*` message inside a subclassed window procedure, calling a brush-creation API such as `CreateSolidBrush` each time the message fires creates a new `HBRUSH` on every paint cycle without releasing the previous one. This leaks GDI handles rapidly --- on a form being continuously resized, the handle count can increase by hundreds per second, eventually crashing the application. The correct pattern is to create the brush once, store the handle in a module-level or class-level variable, return that cached handle from the message handler, and destroy it with `DeleteObject` only when the window is being destroyed.

_Source threads: 1440565935470542908 · confidence: high_

> [!NOTE]
> On Windows 8.1 and older (and some Windows 10 configurations), `Form_DPIChange` fires at unexpected times: when a modal dialog loads, when a modal dialog unloads (immediately after `Form_Unload` completes), and when the main form itself unloads --- even when no DPI change has occurred and the system is running on a single monitor at 96 DPI. > [!NOTE]
> Setting **Width** or **Height** inside a `Form_Resize` handler does not raise the **Resize** event again. In VB6, a programmatic size change inside **Resize** would re-fire the event with the new dimensions, which enabled patterns such as constraining the window to a fixed minimum size. twinBASIC applies the size change visually but does not re-raise **Resize**. Code that relies on this VB6 idiom must be adapted---for example, by reading and enforcing limits at the start of the handler rather than relying on the recursive call.

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC has no built-in mechanism to group non-contiguous controls for bulk property changes. A practical workaround is to assign the same integer value to the `Tag` property of every control in a logical group, then iterate `Me.Controls` and apply the change to controls whose `Tag` matches the target group identifier:
>
> ```tb
> Sub SetGroupEnabled(groupId As Long, fEnabled As Boolean)
>     Dim ctl As Control
>     For Each ctl In Me.Controls
>         If ctl.Tag = CStr(groupId) Then ctl.Enabled = fEnabled
>     Next
> End Sub
> ```
>
> When all the controls are physically together on the form, placing them inside a single container (such as a [**Frame**](../Frame)) and enabling or disabling the container is a simpler alternative.

> [!NOTE]
> **DPIChange requires Windows 8.1 or later.** The underlying `WM_DPICHANGED` message is not available on Windows 7 or earlier; the event is never raised on those systems. twinBASIC declares `PER_MONITOR_DPI_AWARE` automatically, so the event fires whenever the form moves to a monitor with a different DPI.

To compute the new DPI in dots per inch from inside a **DPIChange** handler, use `DpiScaleFactorX` rather than `GetDeviceCaps`. Calling `GetDeviceCaps(GetDC(GetDesktopWindow()), LOGPIXELSX)` on a multi-monitor per-monitor-DPI system always returns 96 and is unreliable. The correct formula is:

```tb
Private Sub Form_DPIChange(NewDPI As Long)
    ' NewDPI == 96 * Me.DpiScaleFactorX
    Dim dblScale As Double
    dblScale = Me.DpiScaleFactorX
    ' rescale fonts, images, etc.
End Sub
```

_Source threads: 1433476500035993620 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-10-30 to 2025-11-21_
_Reviewer note: Content to be inserted after the DPIChange event description (line ~815) and/or after the DpiScaleFactorX property description (line ~197). Confirm that WM_DPICHANGED availability on Windows 8.1+ is accurate and that twinBASIC declares PER_MONITOR_DPI_AWARE by default._

To obtain the full qualified name of a control that may belong to a control array, use an identity check rather than an `On Error` block:

```tb
Dim sName As String
sName = Ctrl.Name
If Not Controls(sName) Is Ctrl Then
    sName = sName & "(" & Ctrl.Index & ")"
End If
```

Indexing **Controls** with a plain string such as `"Picture1(0)"` is not supported (neither in twinBASIC nor in VB6); the identity check above is the canonical workaround.

> **MinWidth** and **MinHeight** accept values in twips, not pixels. A pixel equals 15 twips at 96 DPI, but the exact ratio varies with the system DPI setting. Setting these properties to pixel values will produce a minimum size far smaller than intended. Use `Screen.TwipsPerPixelX` and `Screen.TwipsPerPixelY` to convert pixel measurements at runtime:
>
> ```tb
> Me.MinWidth  = 278 * Screen.TwipsPerPixelX
> Me.MinHeight = 161 * Screen.TwipsPerPixelY
> ```

**MinWidth** and **MinHeight** apply only to user-driven interactive resizing at runtime; they have no effect in the designer.

> [!NOTE]
> When Per-Monitor DPI Awareness is enabled, twinBASIC (matching VB6 behavior) sizes and positions controls in twips relative to the DPI of the monitor the application starts on. If the user drags the form to a monitor with a different DPI, the runtime does not automatically reposition or resize controls. The application must handle the change by responding to the [**DPIChange**](#dpichange) event or by subclassing `WM_DPICHANGED`. The conversion from a new DPI value to the equivalent twips scale factor is: `twips = 1440 / DPI`.

The `Form_DPIChange` event signature includes an optional `rcNewRect As RECT` argument that carries the OS-suggested window rectangle for the new DPI:

```tb
Private Sub Form_DPIChange(ByVal lNewDPI As Long, rcNewRect As RECT)
    ' lNewDPI is the new effective DPI (e.g. 144 for 150% scaling)
    ' rcNewRect is the OS-suggested new client rectangle in screen pixels
    ' Me.DpiScaleFactorX also reflects the new scale after this event fires
End Sub
```

> [!NOTE]
> The order of `DPIChange` relative to `Resize` events depends on how the move was triggered. When code calls `Me.Move`: `DPIChange` fires first, then three `Resize` events follow. When the user drags the form across a monitor boundary: one `Resize` fires at the old DPI, then `DPIChange` fires, then two more `Resize` events fire. Code in `DPIChange` therefore cannot assume the form has reached its final size. Layout that must wait until all resize processing is complete currently requires subclassing `WM_EXITSIZEMOVE`.

> [!NOTE]
> Unlike VB6, twinBASIC has built-in support for automatic control resizing without third-party add-ins. Three mechanisms are available:
>
> - **Anchors** -- per-control properties that tie each edge (left, right, top, bottom) to the corresponding edge of the parent form. Anchoring a control to all four edges stretches it as the form resizes; anchoring only to the right and bottom edges keeps it pinned to the lower-right corner.
> - **Docking** -- attaches a control to one edge of its container so it fills that edge and moves with it.
> - [**MultiFrame**](../MultiFrame) -- divides a layout strip into child [**Frame**](../Frame) controls sized as percentages of the available space; the frames re-lay out automatically whenever the **MultiFrame** is resized.
>
> The [**Resize**](#resize) event is still available for custom layout logic, as in VB6.

> [!NOTE]
> `Set frm = Form1` (without **New**) assigns a reference to the already-running default instance of the form class, including any property values that have been set at run time. Passing a form variable **As Form** also passes a reference --- no copy is made. If property values set in **Form_Activate** are not visible through a form reference, the most common cause is that **Form_Activate** has not fired yet because the form was not yet shown.

> [!NOTE]
> When a shell `IContextMenu`'s Share verb is invoked from a third-party application, the shell queries the host via `IObjectWithSite` for an `IServiceProvider`, then calls `QueryService` for `IOleWindow` to obtain the host window's `HWND`. Without this plumbing, the Share UI appears briefly then immediately closes. The fix is to call `IObjectWithSite.SetSite` on the `IContextMenu` object, passing the form, and to implement `IServiceProvider.QueryService` on the form so that requests for `IID_IOleWindow` return the form's `IOleWindow` interface. twinBASIC forms already implement `IOleWindow` natively, so no separate `IOleWindow` class is needed --- only `IServiceProvider` must be added.
>
> ```tb
> ' After obtaining the IContextMenu:
> Dim s As IObjectWithSite
> Set s = pCtx
> s.SetSite(Me)
> 
> ' In the form (which also Implements IServiceProvider):
> Private Sub IServiceProvider_QueryService(guidService As UUID, riid As UUID, ppvObject As LongPtr) _
>         Implements IServiceProvider.QueryService
>     Dim pUnk As IUnknownUnrestricted
>     If IsEqualGUID(riid, IID_IOleWindow) Then
>         Set pUnk = Me
>         pUnk.QueryInterface IID_IOleWindow, ppvObject
>     Else
>         Err.ReturnHResult = E_NOTIMPL
>     End If
> End Sub
> ```
>
> Even with this fix, the Share UI may not display valid share targets on systems without Microsoft Store apps installed, mirroring Explorer's own fallback behavior on such systems.

## docs/Reference/VB/Form/index.md · example

### Showing the Windows Share UI

To display the Windows Share UI from a twinBASIC Win32 form, subscribe to the `DataRequested` event before calling `ShowShareUIForWindow`. The event fires when the Share UI is displayed --- not when the user picks a target --- so the data to share must be assembled there.

This example uses the WinRT `IDataTransferManagerInterop` and `IDataTransferManager` interfaces from the twinBASIC WinRT package. It works in both 32-bit and 64-bit targets.

```tb
Class frmShare

Implements ITypedEventHandlerDataTransferManagerDataRequested

Private DataTransferManager As IDataTransferManager

Private Sub Form_Load()
    ' Obtain the DataTransferManager for this window and subscribe to DataRequested.
    Set DataTransferManager = CType(Of IDataTransferManagerInterop)(DataTransferManagerStatics) _
        .GetForWindow(hWnd, GetIID(Of IDataTransferManager))
    DataTransferManager.AddDataRequested Me
End Sub

' The event fires when ShowShareUIForWindow displays the dialog.
Private Sub ITypedEventHandlerDataTransferManagerDataRequested_Invoke( _
        ByVal Sender As IDataTransferManager, ByVal Args As IDataRequestedEventArgs)
    With Args.Request.Data
        .Properties.Title = StrRef(App.Title)
        ' Share text:
        .SetText StrRef("Shared from twinBASIC")
        ' To share files instead, call .SetStorageItems with an IIterable_IStorageItem.
    End With
End Sub

Private Sub cmdShare_Click()
    CType(Of IDataTransferManagerInterop)(DataTransferManagerStatics).ShowShareUIForWindow(hWnd)
End Sub

End Class
```

To keep the form class uncluttered, the event handler can be a separate class:

```tb
DataTransferManager.AddDataRequested New cDataTransferManagerEvent(AnyParams)
```

> [!NOTE]
> The Share UI tries to fit within the host form's bounding rectangle. The form must be large enough to accommodate the dialog, or the dialog will be too small to display correctly.

_Source threads: 1384721515542479049 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2026-03-23 to 2026-03-24_

The bug affected projects with native controls such as **CheckBox** and third-party VB6-compatible controls on the same form. It was fixed in BETA 765. If upgrading is not immediately possible, compiling the project twice in a row without any code change between attempts is a confirmed workaround -- the second compile consistently succeeds.

## docs/Reference/VB/Form/index.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> **Aligned-control layout deviations from VB6.** Two known differences affect controls that use the **Align** property to dock to form edges:
>
> - **Layout priority.** In VB6, top-aligned and bottom-aligned controls always take priority in the docking calculation: they stretch to the full form width first, and left-aligned and right-aligned controls then fill the remaining height. In twinBASIC, priority follows control creation order instead of alignment direction. A left-aligned or right-aligned control created before a top-aligned or bottom-aligned control takes priority, producing a layout that differs from VB6. The developer confirmed this will be corrected in a future release. To replicate VB6 behaviour in the meantime, cut and paste controls in the designer to adjust their creation order so that top-aligned and bottom-aligned controls are created before left-aligned and right-aligned ones.
>
> - **Hiding aligned controls.** When a docked (aligned) control is hidden at run time --- or when an aligned control starts hidden at application startup --- neither the hidden control nor the parent form repaints correctly. This is a known bug as of mid-2026. Calling `Me.Refresh` after hiding an aligned control is a partial workaround.

## docs/Reference/VB/Frame/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1155870717070541001, 1322865080446222398, 1392533930351001801, 1463861745100656751, 1219422930862084136, 1384838697614049351, 1415566731455500399]

> [!NOTE]
> **Design-mode rendering limitation:** windowless controls --- such as [**Label**](../Label) and [**Image**](../Image) --- placed inside a **Frame** are not rendered in the twinBASIC form designer. The controls are present and function correctly in the compiled output, but remain invisible in the IDE's visual designer. This is a known open bug.
>
> The workaround is to use a [**PictureBox**](../PictureBox) as the container instead. Controls inside a **PictureBox** render normally in design mode.
>
> When moving controls from a **Frame** to a **PictureBox** via cut-and-paste in the designer, twinBASIC may convert the pasted control into a control array, generating errors and potentially freezing the IDE. If this occurs, use Undo to trigger a Resync and then remove the unwanted array index.

> [!NOTE]
> If a **Frame** is included in a multi-selection when copying controls, subsequently pasting additional controls can cause the pasted controls to become children of the **Frame** rather than children of the form. To avoid this, ensure the form surface (not a frame) is the active container before pasting. This behavior was fixed in BETA 853.

When a control is selected in the designer but positioned outside the visible area of the form (for example, after being pasted with coordinates that place it off-screen), it cannot be dragged back into view because clicking elsewhere deselects it. The confirmed workaround is to type new values for the **Left** and **Top** properties directly in the Properties window -- setting both to `0` moves the control to the top-left corner while keeping its size.

## docs/Reference/VB/Frame/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1155870717070541001, 1322865080446222398, 1324659889280258159, 1392533930351001801, 1463861745100656751, 1219422930862084136, 1415566731455500399]

> [!NOTE]
> **Frame** does not raise a **Resize** event. If child controls inside a frame need to respond dynamically to the container being resized --- for example to implement a custom layout that repositions or resizes its children in code --- use a [**PictureBox**](../PictureBox) instead, because **PictureBox** does raise **Resize**. This is a VB6 limitation that carries over to twinBASIC. For declarative automatic layout, twinBASIC's built-in [**Anchors**](#anchors) and [**Dock**](#dock) work with **Frame**, **PictureBox**, **UserControl**, and **Form** as containers; the absence of a **Frame** **Resize** event is only relevant when custom resize logic is needed in a code handler.

## docs/Reference/VB/Global/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1289730701087866941, 1315857533772107839, 1213599044912287865, 1435977539532230657, 1448886359707353248, 1455614957738790943, 1461395463310938175]

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC versions before BETA 366, string table entries with IDs above 32,767 --- the upper limit of a signed 16-bit **Integer** --- caused a native access-violation crash during compilation, with no diagnostic message. The Win32 `STRINGTABLE` format stores IDs as an unsigned 16-bit value (range 0--65,535), and **LoadResString** accepts a **Long**, so IDs in the upper half of the unsigned range are valid in principle. Earlier compiler builds treated the ID internally as a signed integer, triggering the crash. This was corrected in BETA 366. Keep all string table IDs at or below 32,767 when targeting older builds.

> [!NOTE]
> The bare, unqualified `LoadPicture` call uses the same underlying API as VB6, which does not support modern image formats such as PNG at run time. Passing a PNG path to unqualified `LoadPicture` raises run-time error 481 (*Invalid picture*), even though the same file loads correctly when assigned through the Properties window at design time. To load PNG files from code, qualify the call explicitly: `Global.LoadPicture(path)`. JPEG files work with either form. ## docs/Reference/VB/Global/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1131491832367415306, 1289730701087866941, 1213599044912287865, 1435977539532230657, 1448886359707353248, 1455614957738790943, 1461395463310938175]

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC provides two forms of `LoadPicture`. The unqualified form (`LoadPicture`) is the VB6-compatible version and does not support PNG files. To load a PNG image --- including from a resource byte array returned by `LoadResData` --- use the explicitly qualified form `Global.LoadPicture`:
> 
> ```tb
> Dim ThePicture As StdPicture
> Set ThePicture = Global.LoadPicture(LoadResData("THUMBNAIL", "CUSTOM"))
> ```
> 
> Without the `Global.` qualifier, PNG loading fails silently or returns an empty picture.

## docs/Reference/VB/Global/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1131491832367415306, 1289730701087866941, 1315857533772107839, 1435977539532230657, 1448886359707353248, 1455614957738790943, 1461395463310938175]

> [!NOTE]
> When a project references `stdole2.tlb` (which is common in VB6 imports), calling `LoadPicture` without qualification resolves to stdole's version rather than twinBASIC's built-in implementation. stdole's version does not accept a byte array and raises a "Path/File access error" when passed one. The fix is to call `Global.LoadPicture` explicitly, which routes to twinBASIC's implementation and supports byte arrays and PNG images with transparency.
>
> To load a PNG stored in the project's resources: add the PNG file under a folder named `CUSTOM` in the Resources editor, load it into a byte array with `LoadResData("name", "CUSTOM")`, then pass the byte array to `Global.LoadPicture`.

> [!NOTE]
> `LoadResPicture` only supports images stored in the standard `BITMAP` resource folder. Attempting to load a PNG resource with `LoadResPicture` fails at runtime. PNG images must be stored under a custom resource folder name (e.g. `CUSTOM`) and retrieved with `LoadResData`, then passed to `Global.LoadPicture`.

## docs/Reference/VB/Global/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1131491832367415306, 1289730701087866941, 1315857533772107839, 1213599044912287865, 1435977539532230657, 1448886359707353248, 1461395463310938175]

> [!NOTE]
> When running under the twinBASIC IDE (F5), calling the Win32 API **LoadStringW** via a **Declare** statement always returns 0 and writes a NUL byte at the start of the buffer, because no real `hInstance` exists during IDE execution. The built-in resource-loading functions --- **LoadResString**, **LoadResPicture**, and **LoadResData** --- have simulated implementations that work correctly in the IDE. This matches VB6 IDE behaviour. Code that calls **LoadStringW** directly must be compiled to an EXE before it will work.

> [!NOTE]
> **LoadResString** determines which language variant of a string resource to load by calling `GetUserDefaultLCID()` on every invocation --- the value is not cached. It does not read the locale set with `SetThreadLocale`. When the user-default LCID does not match an available resource language, it falls back to the neutral-language variant.

## docs/Reference/VB/Global/index.md · example

To load a UTF-8 text resource (for example a JSON file stored under a custom resource type) and convert it to a twinBASIC string:

```tb
Dim b() As Byte
b = LoadResData("config.json", "DATA")
Dim s As String = StrConv(b, vbFromUTF8)
```

`LoadResData` returns the raw bytes of the embedded resource. Because twinBASIC's native **String** type is UTF-16, a UTF-8 resource file must be decoded with `StrConv(..., vbFromUTF8)` before use as a string.

> [!NOTE]
> The twinBASIC **ListBox**, like the VB6 **ListBox**, uses tab-separated text in item strings to simulate column-aligned display rather than true multi-column layout. It does not replicate the behavior of the Microsoft Access **ListBox**, which supports SQL row sources, bound columns, and true multi-column data display. For Access-style multi-column list UIs, the [**ListView**](../../WinNativeCommonCtls/ListView/) control from the WinNativeCommonCtls package is a closer substitute.

## docs/Reference/VB/ListBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1213808258133786686, 1255041798103896104, 1164183134460457010, 1349636197038948403]

> [!NOTE]
> The twinBASIC **ListBox** is based on the VB6 forms system, not the Microsoft Forms 2.0 system used by VBA UserForms in Excel. Properties found on the MSForms `ListBox` --- such as `ColumnCount` and `ColumnWidths`, which control an independently-sized multi-column layout --- are not available. The [**Columns**](#columns) property provides a tab-stop-based column layout where the column width is determined by dividing the control's pixel width by the number of columns; independent per-column widths are not supported. For a true multi-column list with separate, configurable column widths, use the [**ListView**](../../WinNativeCommonCtls/ListView/) control from the WinNativeCommonCtls package.

## docs/Reference/VB/MDIForm/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1050531812771897445, 1457226482924654754, 1241159205092855808, 1354723368607416430, 1463921097509699729]

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, closing the MDI parent does not raise **Form_Unload** on open MDI child forms. The [**QueryUnload**](#queryunload) event fires on each child (in sequence) before it fires on the parent, so child cleanup that cancels the close must use **QueryUnload**. In VB6, both **QueryUnload** and **Unload** fired on each child during parent close; twinBASIC raises only **QueryUnload** on the children. Code that relies on **Form_Unload** in MDI children for cleanup or save logic will not execute on application exit.

_Source threads: 1251158664287617097 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-06-14 to 2025-04-11_
_Reviewer note: This is a confirmed twinBASIC deviation from VB6 with a reproducible test case per the Discord thread. Placement: add this NOTE to the Unload event section, or to the Lifecycle table at the top of the page, as a deviation callout. The Lifecycle table already notes QueryUnload fires on children before the parent; the Unload event description does not mention the missing child-Unload behavior. Consider whether the existing QueryUnload event description (which correctly describes the cascade) should also cross-reference this deviation._

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> Declare MDI form variables with the specific concrete class type, not the generic **Form** type. Storing an MDI form instance in a variable declared as `Form` and then instantiating it with `New` causes an ACCESS_VIOLATION crash inside `MDIForm.Class_BeforeFirstMethodAccess` at startup. This can occur even in projects that ran correctly under VB6.
>
> ```tb
> ' Correct: use the specific class type
> Public frmMainForm As frmMain
> Set frmMainForm = New frmMain
>
> ' Incorrect: triggers an ACCESS_VIOLATION
> ' Public frmMainForm As Form
> ' Set frmMainForm = New frmMain
> ```

> [!NOTE]
> There is no `MDIChildForms` collection on **MDIForm**. To iterate open MDI children, use the global **Forms** collection and skip the MDI parent by testing with `TypeOf`:
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub CloseAllChildren()
>     Dim f As Form
>     For Each f In Forms
>         If (TypeOf f Is VB.MDIForm) = False Then
>             Unload f
>         End If
>     Next
> End Sub
> ```

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC applies **Align** property layout in the creation order of the controls, rather than giving top- and bottom-aligned controls priority over left- and right-aligned ones as VB6 does. If the layout differs from VB6, reorder the controls in the designer (cut and paste changes creation order) so that top/bottom-aligned controls are created before left/right-aligned ones. VB6 compatibility for this ordering is planned for a future update.

> [!NOTE]
> Hiding a control whose **Align** property is set does not correctly repaint the vacated area or refresh the MDI form client area. The same problem occurs at application startup when some aligned controls start invisible. This is a known twinBASIC issue; a fix to match VB6 behavior is planned.

> [!NOTE]
> Adding elements to a menu control array with [**Load**](../../../Core/Load) at runtime is significantly slower in twinBASIC than in VB6. Applications that load large menus dynamically at startup may see noticeable delays. Where possible, define menu control array elements at design time in the menu editor rather than adding them with **Load** at runtime. Where runtime population is unavoidable, keep the number of dynamically loaded items to a minimum.

## docs/Reference/VB/Menu/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1223281676776374424, 1283687691585716244, 1359662182807240874, 1404378228528906275, 1418252916833259721, 1493553704803238058]

> [!NOTE]
> Some VB6 code uses `VarType(controlArray(i))` to test whether a control array element has been loaded before calling **Load**. This technique does not work reliably in twinBASIC and raises run-time error 340 (*Control array element does not exist*). The correct cross-compatible pattern is to compare the loop index against `controlArray.UBound` and load a new element only when the index exceeds the current upper bound:
>
> ```tb
> If i > mnuMain.UBound Then Load mnuMain(i)
> mnuMain(i).Caption = MenuCaptions(i)
> ```
>
> This pattern works in both VB6 and twinBASIC.

> [!NOTE]
> When displaying a menu via [**Form.PopUpMenu**](../Form/#popupmenu) while the form's menu bar is hidden, icons assigned through the Win32 **SetMenuItemBitmaps** API do not appear. Use the menu item's [**Picture**](#picture) property instead --- twinBASIC's own menu rendering handles icon display correctly in both menu-bar and pop-up contexts.
>
> PNG images assigned to [**Picture**](#picture) may show rendering artifacts around semi-transparent edges when the menu is opened with the mouse; ICO format is more reliable for transparent icons.
>
> As of April 2026, [**IconSizeX**](#iconsizex) and [**IconSizeY**](#iconsizey) are reported as non-functional. Set [**Picture**](#picture) to an image already sized at the intended pixel dimensions rather than relying on these properties to select a resolution from a multi-resolution `.ico`.

The root cause is related to the `E_NOINTERFACE` error in the `Parent` property being silently consumed in the paint path, leaving the control in an incorrect painted state. > [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC requires a **PictureBox** to belong to a visible form before drawing methods ([**PSet**](#pset), [**Line**](#line), [**Circle**](#circle), and so on) produce any output. In VB6, drawing on a form that has been loaded but never shown works correctly; in twinBASIC the calls produce no visible result in that state. The workaround is to call **Show** on the form before drawing, then immediately set **Visible** = **False** if the form must remain hidden. This applies to the common VB6 pattern of using a hidden off-screen form as a drawing buffer whose contents are later copied to a visible window via **BitBlt** or [**PaintPicture**](#paintpicture).

>
> ```tb
> Declare PtrSafe Function GetPixel Lib "gdi32" _
>     (ByVal hDC As LongPtr, ByVal x As Long, ByVal y As Long) As Long
> ```
>
> When [**ScaleMode**](#scalemode) is `vbPixels`, `GetPixel(pic.hDC, x, y)` returns the same colour value as `pic.Point(x, y)` would in VB6. For other scale modes, convert coordinates first: multiply `x` by `Screen.TwipsPerPixelX` and `y` by `Screen.TwipsPerPixelY` before passing them to `GetPixel`.

## docs/Reference/VB/PictureBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1054022348245848145, 1054022348245848145, 1056321299787567175, 1056321299787567175, 1109318483969318932, 1109318483969318932, 1109318483969318932, 1159840322382204968, 1160188802711691344, 1173678952062132224, 1173967867566366730, 1173967867566366730, 1231957953352044626, 1245451555306475614, 1324659889280258159, 1328793719738204251, 1345329179893174303, 1360408738699153549, 1367651337231274024, 1381263527569784935, 1388546772401393724, 1400217886899048520, 1457482996033786153, 1495344809282633859, 1470946214869598230, 1126749039103332443, 1153656809425473637, 1367648395933646929]

> [!NOTE]
> **PaintPicture** relies on **BitBlt** internally and has no concept of alpha transparency. When a PNG image with transparency is drawn through **PaintPicture**, the alpha channel is discarded and artefacting appears. To composite a semi-transparent image onto a surface, call the Win32 `AlphaBlend` API directly, passing the picture box's [**hDC**](#hdc) as the destination. `AlphaBlend` can also scale the source, but the output quality is limited because it uses `SetStretchBltMode` on the destination device context. For icon-based **StdPicture** objects, `DrawIconEx` is an alternative that preserves transparency and supports resizing (the interpolation quality is not documented). For high-quality scaling of alpha-transparent images, the recommended approach is to use the Windows Imaging Component (WIC) with fant or bicubic interpolation via Win32 API calls, or to use GDI+ --- read the PNG as a byte stream, create a GDI+ Image object from the stream, scale it with GDI+, and convert back to a **StdPicture**.

## docs/Reference/VB/PictureBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1054022348245848145, 1054022348245848145, 1056321299787567175, 1056321299787567175, 1109318483969318932, 1109318483969318932, 1109318483969318932, 1159840322382204968, 1160188802711691344, 1173678952062132224, 1173967867566366730, 1173967867566366730, 1231957953352044626, 1245451555306475614, 1324659889280258159, 1328793719738204251, 1345329179893174303, 1360408738699153549, 1367651337231274024, 1381263527569784935, 1388546772401393724, 1400217886899048520, 1457482996033786153, 1495344809282633859, 1470946214869598230, 1126749039103332443, 1153656809425473637, 1367648395933646929]

> [!NOTE]
> A **PictureBox** can host a WinRT Image control (no XAML required) as a hardware-accelerated alternative for displaying images. The WinRT Image control supports any format that **LoadPicture** accepts, including PNG with full alpha transparency and animated GIFs. It supports four stretch modes: **None** (0, original size), **Fill** (1, fills the destination ignoring aspect ratio), **Uniform** (2, fills the destination preserving aspect ratio), and **UniformToFill** (3, fills the destination preserving aspect ratio but clips the source when the ratios differ). Images can also be loaded from a URL; loading is asynchronous and completion is signalled through **ImageOpened** and **ImageFailed** events.

## docs/Reference/VB/PictureBox/index.md · example

### PictureBox as a tab-page container

A **PictureBox** can serve as a tab-page container when used together with a **TabStrip** from the WinNativeCommonCtls package (VBCCR). Each page is a **PictureBox** with [**BorderStyle**](#borderstyle) set to **vbNoBorder**; all pages except the first have [**Visible**](#visible) set to **False** at design time. Child controls are placed inside each picture box, and the picture boxes are dragged onto the **TabStrip** in the designer so they overlay it.

```tb
Private Sub Form_Load() Handles Form.Load
    TabStrip1.Tabs(1).Caption = "Tab 1"
    TabStrip1.Tabs.Add , , "Tab 2"
End Sub

Private Sub TabStrip1_TabClick(ByVal TabItem As TbsTab) Handles TabStrip1.TabClick
    If TabItem.Index = 1 Then
        pbPage1.Visible = True
        pbPage2.Visible = False
    ElseIf TabItem.Index = 2 Then
        pbPage1.Visible = False
        pbPage2.Visible = True
    End If
End Sub
```

When the **TabStrip** has visual styles enabled, setting the picture box [**BackColor**](#backcolor) to white makes the page background match the control's themed appearance.

## docs/Reference/VB/Printer/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1258198304408342600]

## VB6 compatibility: `Implements Printer`

Porting VB6 code that uses `Implements Printer` requires manual adjustments because the twinBASIC **Printer** class differs from the VB6 Printer interface in two ways.

> [!NOTE]
> The datatype mismatches described below and the overloaded-`New` issue are known bugs confirmed by the twinBASIC maintainer. They are expected to be corrected in a future release.

### Datatype mismatches

Several method parameters use different numeric types in the twinBASIC **Printer** class compared to the original VB6 Printer object interface --- primarily **Integer** in VB6 where twinBASIC declares **Long**, and **Single** in VB6 where twinBASIC declares **Double**. When another class uses `Implements Printer`, the compiler checks all parameter types against the declared interface; any mismatch produces a type-mismatch compile error. All mismatched types must be corrected manually in the implementing class.

### Extra members not present in the VB6 interface

The twinBASIC **Printer** class exposes three members that have no counterpart in the VB6 Printer interface: `Property Get OutputFile() As String`, `Property Let OutputFile(File As String)`, and `Property Let Font(ByVal Value As StdFont)`. A class that uses `Implements Printer` must also implement these three members to satisfy the compiler.

### Overloaded constructors and COM type library generation

The twinBASIC **Printer** class defines two overloaded `New` constructors (`Sub New()` and `Sub New(DeviceName As String, DriverPart As String, Port As String)`). When another class uses `Implements Printer`, the compiler also requires those `New` methods to be implemented. However, COM does not support overloaded methods, so when the project has `Attribute VB_Exposed = True` twinBASIC cannot generate the type library and reports errors such as:

```
[TYPELIB] failed to create typelibrary interface procedure names '_cVBDraw.Printer_New'.
[TYPELIB] failed to set coclass inheritence on 'cVBDraw'.
```

The only workaround is to open `Printer.twin` directly from the IDE's packages folder and remove the two overloaded `New` methods before compiling the dependent project.

_Date range: 2025-01-28 to 2025-02-03_

## docs/Reference/VB/Printer/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1333587859474747413]

> [!NOTE]
> Output methods --- [**Print**](#print), [**EndDoc**](#enddoc), and the other drawing methods --- only work on the implicit **Printer** global. Calling them on a `Printer` variable obtained by iterating the [**Printers**](../Printers/) collection raises run-time error 438. The correct pattern is to identify the desired printer by iterating **Printers**, assign it with `Set Printer = p`, and then call all output methods on the **Printer** global.
>
> Starting with BETA 571, the [**Printers**](../Printers/) collection supports name-based lookup (`Set Printer = Printers("Microsoft Print to PDF")`), which is a twinBASIC extension not present in VB6.
>
> If [**OutputFile**](#outputfile) points to a folder that does not exist, the PDF print driver fails silently with a generic printer error. Ensure the destination folder exists before setting **OutputFile**.
>
> The [**Print**](#print) method does not appear in IntelliSense for the **Printer** object (nor for **Form**); this is a known display omission and does not prevent the method from working.

## docs/Reference/VB/Screen/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1047796050485858354, 1247164784080720005, 1422507930057445499]

> [!NOTE]
> In VB6, `Screen.TwipsPerPixelX` and `Screen.TwipsPerPixelY` return `15` on a standard 96-DPI display (1440 twips per logical inch ÷ 96 pixels per inch). In twinBASIC these properties return `10` on the same display, matching a 144-DPI computation. Code ported from VB6 that multiplies pixel values by `Screen.TwipsPerPixelX` or `Screen.TwipsPerPixelY` will produce differently sized controls in twinBASIC. Switch the control's **ScaleMode** to `vbPixels` and remove the `TwipsPerPixelX`/`TwipsPerPixelY` multiplier to correct the sizing.

## docs/Reference/VB/TextBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1058331987909287996, 1116569721786073148, 1165582099772887070, 1078023402998202449, 1289442595369386025, 1297367528720437308, 1501562581792460870, 1184567325689651351, 1361779990420783306]

> [!NOTE]
> **TextHint** has no effect when [**MultiLine**](#multiline) is **True**. The Win32 `EM_SETCUEBANNER` message is ignored for multiline edit controls, so the placeholder text never appears regardless of the **TextHint** value. A workaround is to leave **MultiLine** as **False** at design time and toggle it dynamically in the [**Change**](#change) event: set **MultiLine** to **False** (restoring the hint) when [**Text**](#text) is empty, and to **True** (enabling multiline input) once the user has typed something.

```tb
Private Sub Text1_Change()
    If Text1.Text = "" Then
        Text1.MultiLine = False   ' restore cue banner
    Else
        Text1.MultiLine = True    ' switch to multiline input
    End If
End Sub
```

> [!NOTE]
> **VB.TextBox** does not have an `AfterUpdate` event. The `AfterUpdate` event belongs to `Access.TextBox` and is specific to Microsoft Access --- it cannot be used in twinBASIC. To detect that a text box value has been committed by the user, combine the [**GotFocus**](#gotfocus) and [**LostFocus**](#lostfocus) events (storing the value on focus gain and comparing on focus loss), or use [**Change**](#change) together with [**LostFocus**](#lostfocus) if per-keystroke tracking is also needed.

## docs/Reference/VB/TextBox/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1058331987909287996, 1116569721786073148, 1165582099772887070, 1260413774398226518, 1078023402998202449, 1289442595369386025, 1501562581792460870, 1184567325689651351, 1361779990420783306]

> [!NOTE]
> The [**Validate**](#validate) event is not a drop-in replacement for the `AfterUpdate` event found in Microsoft Access. Two behavioral differences are worth noting:
>
> 1. **Validate** does not fire when focus moves to a control whose [**CausesValidation**](#causesvalidation) is **False** --- this is by design so that a Cancel button does not trigger validation.
> 2. If the user tabs from the validated control to a `CausesValidation = False` control and then to another control, **Validate** fires against the originally validated control when the second control receives focus, not when the `CausesValidation = False` control received it. This requires additional state in the containing control to handle correctly.
>
> For behavior equivalent to `AfterUpdate`, write handlers in [**KeyUp**](#keyup), [**LostFocus**](#lostfocus), or both, on the individual control, and optionally on the containing **UserControl**'s **LostFocus** event.

> The **TextBox** control, when used in RTF mode, does not expose a dedicated event for hyperlink clicks. > [!NOTE]
> The shell API `SHLimitInputEdit`, which restricts the characters a user can type into a TextBox to an allow-list or exclude-list, was reported as non-functional in twinBASIC as of late 2023. The undocumented `SHLimitInputEditWithFlags` (which calls `SHLimitInputEdit` internally) provides a wider set of filtering options and does not require implementing a COM interface. Both APIs and their supporting types are available through the community **tbShellLib** library.
>
> When using the custom-character-filter option of `SHLimitInputEditWithFlags`, note that although the filter parameter is declared as `LPWSTR`, the API accepts only ANSI data. Passing `StrPtr(myString)` directly does not work; convert the string to ANSI first:
>
> ```tb
> ' Correct: convert to ANSI before passing
> SHLimitInputEditWithFlags hWnd, SHILEF_RESTRICT_CHARS, StrPtr(StrConv(allowedChars, vbFromUnicode))
> ```

> [!NOTE]
> When using the Win32 `IAutoComplete` interface with the `AutoCompleteOptionUseTab` flag, the Tab key is not treated as an input key while the autocomplete drop-down is open if the intrinsic **TextBox** control is used. To work around this, use the `VBCCR.TextBoxW` control instead and handle its `PreviewKeyDown` event: set `IsInputKey` to `True` when `KeyCode` equals `vbKeyTab` and the autocomplete object's `DroppedDown()` returns `True`.
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub TextBoxW1_PreviewKeyDown(ByVal KeyCode As Integer, IsInputKey As Boolean)
>     If KeyCode = vbKeyTab Then IsInputKey = MyAutoComplete.DroppedDown()
> End Sub
> ```
>
> Without this workaround, the Tab key dismisses the drop-down rather than selecting the current suggestion.

## docs/Reference/VB/Timer/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1091707854488096851, 1119744425015386213, 1459967523435974857, 1477515216680911000, 1459951406503952538]

> [!NOTE]
> Timer events and modal dialogs interact differently depending on where the dialog is opened. If `MsgBox` (or another modal dialog) is called from code *outside* the **Timer** event handler --- for example from a button click while the timer is running --- the timer continues to fire while the dialog is open: each tick is delivered to the message pump in the normal way. If `MsgBox` is called from *within* the **Timer** handler itself, reentrancy protection prevents the handler from being entered again until the current invocation returns; the pending tick is discarded.
>
> The VB6 IDE suppressed timer events during any `MsgBox`, regardless of call origin, which gave a misleading impression of compiled behavior. A compiled VB6 executable (native or p-code) always allowed external-MsgBox ticks through. twinBASIC targets the compiled behavior: as of BETA 330, the IDE and the compiled output are consistent --- timers fire during an externally-invoked modal dialog and are blocked by reentrancy only when the dialog originates from within the handler itself.

_Source threads: 1118258272152059997 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-06-13 to 2023-06-14_

> [!NOTE]
> In VB6, a `Declare` statement naming the Win32 `SetFocus` API without an `Alias` clause (for example, `Declare Function SetFocus Lib "user32" (ByVal hWnd As LongPtr) As LongPtr`) inside a **UserControl** module compiles and resolves to the API. In twinBASIC prior to BETA 203, the same declaration produces a compile error: *unable to disambiguate between overloaded methods in call to 'SetFocus'*, because both the inherited built-in method and the `Declare`-based API are in scope with the same name. The workaround is to add an `Alias` clause to the `Declare` statement so it has a distinct callable name:
>
> ```tb
> Declare Function SetFocusAPI Lib "user32" Alias "SetFocus" (ByVal hWnd As LongPtr) As LongPtr
> ```
>
> A regular `Sub` or `Function` named `SetFocus` does not trigger this error --- it correctly overrides the inherited built-in. The asymmetry between `Declare`-based and `Sub`/`Function`-based name shadowing was fixed in BETA 203.

> [!NOTE]
> In the twinBASIC form designer, a **UserControl** instance is not kept alive between renders. Each time the designer needs to paint the control --- including during a resize drag --- it creates a fresh instance: [**Initialize**](#initialize) fires, property-lets are replayed for any properties that changed, and the instance is discarded. [**Initialize**](#initialize) and [**WriteProperties**](#writeproperties) can therefore fire many times in rapid succession while the user drags a resize handle in design mode. Code that assumes **Initialize** fires once per design-mode session --- for example, a module-level boolean guard set inside **Initialize** --- will misbehave because the guard resets on each new instance. This behavior differs from VB6, where the designer holds the control instance open.

> [!NOTE]
> [**Resize**](#resize) fires continuously while the user holds the mouse button and drags a resize handle in design mode. In VB6, Resize and Paint fire only after the mouse button is released. Some of the intermediate **Resize** events report [**ScaleWidth**](#scalewidth) and [**ScaleHeight**](#scaleheight) as zero even though the control is not zero-sized. A Resize handler that repositions child windows based on these properties must guard against zero values; otherwise child controls may be sized to zero and appear to vanish. The recommended guard is:

```tb
Private Sub UserControl_Resize()
    If ScaleWidth = 0 Or ScaleHeight = 0 Then Exit Sub
    ' reposition child controls here
End Sub
```

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC versions before BETA 218, **TextWidth** could return different measurements for the same string and font depending on the calling context. Calling it from a subclassed window procedure (for example, inside a `WM_MOUSEMOVE` handler via a subclassing callback) and from a native VB event handler (such as a child control's **MouseMove** event) on the same **UserControl** could produce different pixel widths for the same text. This caused visible layout instability when panel sizes were recalculated on each mouse-move message. The issue was fixed in BETA 218.

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC versions before BETA 232, user-defined events raised inside a **UserControl** during the initialization sequence (for example, events fired by a child control's activity before the host's `ReadProperties` call completed) were delivered to the host form's event handlers immediately, even while the control's internal state was still being set up. In VB6, `FreezeEvents` suppresses both built-in and user-defined events during this window; in twinBASIC, `FreezeEvents` previously applied only to built-in events such as **GotFocus**, leaving user-defined events unguarded. This mismatch could cause host-side event handlers to call back into the control before its fields were initialized, producing *object not set* errors or re-entrant initialization. The suppression was extended to cover user-defined events in BETA 232, bringing twinBASIC into line with VB6 behavior. The [**EventsFrozen**](#eventsfrozen) property reflects the current freeze state.

> [!NOTE]
> When implementing `IOleInPlaceActiveObject` (exposed to twinBASIC as `IOleIPAO`) in a custom control extender CoClass, the `IOleIPAO_TranslateAccelerator` method must return `S_FALSE` via `Err.ReturnHResult` for every message it does not handle. Returning `S_OK` signals to the twinBASIC extender that the message was consumed. If a message such as `WM_PAINT` is incorrectly consumed --- returning `S_OK` without actually painting --- Windows re-posts it immediately, creating an endless message loop. Prior to BETA 236, the twinBASIC extender passed all messages to `TranslateAccelerator`, including `WM_PAINT` and `WM_MOUSEMOVE`; BETA 236 corrected this by restricting the messages forwarded to `TranslateAccelerator` to key events only. The built-in [**PreKeyEvents**](#prekeyevents) property provides the same key-interception behaviour without requiring a custom `IOleInPlaceActiveObject` implementation.

> [!NOTE]
> At design time, a **UserControl** has no container, so **Width** and **Height** always report their values in Twips regardless of the [**ScaleMode**](#scalemode) setting. This matches VB6 behaviour. [**ScaleWidth**](#scalewidth) and [**ScaleHeight**](#scaleheight) are the properties that reflect the coordinate system set by **ScaleMode** --- inspect those to observe a custom scale in effect.

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC stores coordinate values (**Width**, **Height**, **ScaleWidth**, **ScaleHeight**, and similar) as **Double** precision internally, whereas VB6 used **Single** precision. As a result, the IDE may display a value with a small floating-point error when an integer is entered --- for example, entering `233` can appear as `232.9999999999995`. This does not affect runtime behaviour.

> [!NOTE]
> Setting `UserControl.Width` or `UserControl.Height` inside `UserControl_Resize` causes **Resize** to fire more times than in VB6. VB6 fires the event again only when the assigned dimension differs from the previous value, resulting in at most two firings for a pattern that constrains one dimension while the other is being changed. In twinBASIC (confirmed in BETA 285) the same pattern fires the event additional times. The same excess-firing behaviour applies to other controls that constrain their height during resize, such as **ComboBox** and **DriveListBox**. A workaround is to guard the assignment so it runs only when the dimension actually needs to change:
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub UserControl_Resize()
>     Dim newH As Long
>     newH = UserControl.ScaleY(UserControl.Width, vbTwips, vbTwips) \ 2  ' example: fix aspect ratio
>     If UserControl.Height <> newH Then
>         UserControl.Height = newH
>     End If
> End Sub
> ```

> [!NOTE]
> When importing a VB6 project (`.vbp`) into twinBASIC, renaming the twinBASIC project away from the original VBP project name can cause a "Failed to deserialize JSON" error when forms that host **UserControl** instances are opened. The error occurs because the imported form data still references each **UserControl** by its old project-qualified name (for example, `Project1.UserControl1`), which no longer matches the renamed project. BETA 283 corrects this automatically: the importer strips the old project-name prefix and replaces it with the internal `$.` prefix (so `Project1.UserControl1` becomes `$.UserControl1`), allowing the compiler to resolve the reference correctly. In earlier builds, the workaround is to delete the broken **UserControl** instance from the form and place a fresh one.

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, the *X* and *Y* parameters of mouse events (**MouseDown**, **MouseMove**, **MouseUp**) on a windowless (lightweight) **UserControl** are expressed in the control's own [**ScaleMode**](#scalemode) units, not always in twips. If [**ScaleMode**](#scalemode) is **vbPixels**, mouse coordinates arrive in pixels. Code that assumes twip coordinates --- for example, `PtInRect` comparisons using twip-scaled rectangles --- behaves incorrectly in that case. Windowed (heavyweight) controls are not affected. This deviation from VB6 behavior was corrected in BETA 303.

> [!NOTE]
> The twinBASIC IDE designer does not currently reproduce the VB6 SP6 lifecycle event order exactly. Known deviations:
> 
> - **ReadProperties** and **WriteProperties** fire during a design-time resize, when only **Paint** (and **Resize** if the dimensions changed) should fire.
> - **ReadProperties** does not fire when the IDE terminates while a form containing the control is open in the designer, but it should.
> - Changing a property at design time causes **ReadProperties** and **WriteProperties** to fire, when only **Paint** (and **Resize** if width or height changed) should fire.
> - Placing a new **UserControl** instance on a form causes **Resize** to fire twice instead of **Show**, and **WriteProperties** and **Terminate** fire when they should not.
> - Opening a form in the designer that contains a **UserControl** causes **WriteProperties** and **Terminate** to fire at the end, when they should not.
> 
> The correct VB6 SP6 event order when opening a designer form is: **Initialize**, **ReadProperties**, **Resize**, **Show**, **Paint**. The correct order when placing a new instance is: **Initialize**, **InitProperties**, **Resize**, **Show**, **Paint**. Note that VB6 without SP6 fired **Resize** before **ReadProperties** on **Show**; SP6 corrected this so **ReadProperties** fires before **Resize**.

> [!NOTE]
> When a **UserControl** creates a child window via `CreateWindowEx` and routes input focus to it by calling the Win32 `SetFocus` API directly, the OLE in-place activation mechanism in the host container is bypassed. In VBA host environments such as Excel or Word UserForms, the container loses track of which control has focus: the child window appears active but does not accept keyboard input until the user clicks it with the mouse. The twinBASIC form host compensates for this internally, so the same code works correctly when the ActiveX is tested on a twinBASIC form --- the disparity only appears in external host containers.
>
> The correct approach is to implement the `IOleInPlaceActiveObject` interface pattern (IPAO) so the host is notified through COM channels when focus moves to the API-created window. Krool's VB Common Controls Replacement (VBCCR) project demonstrates this technique in `VTableHandle.bas`. When the control hosts multiple API-created windows alongside intrinsic controls, Tab-order navigation between them must be tracked manually: the control is responsible for detecting when focus reaches the first or last window in sequence and returning it to the host container.

> [!NOTE]
> Adding a module-level variable to a large **UserControl** (roughly 1 500 lines or more, especially in a project referencing a large package) has been observed to trigger `ACCESS_VIOLATION` native exceptions in the IDE's background compiler threads. When such an exception occurs, the IDE automatically activates TRACE-MODE for additional diagnostic information on subsequent exceptions; TRACE-MODE degrades IntelliSense performance and must be disabled manually via the **Help** menu. The IDE recovers by restarting from the last saved project state.

> [!NOTE]
> Resizing a **UserControl** in the twinBASIC designer by a small amount can, in some configurations, cause child controls to grow dramatically in size and be repositioned far outside the control surface. Controls not placed in the top-left corner are most affected. The issue is associated with anchor properties on the child controls. Recovery requires manually correcting the affected controls' positions and sizes in the designer.

> [!NOTE]
> When a **UserControl** compiled with twinBASIC is hosted in Microsoft Access and the user switches directly from Design View to Form View (without closing and reopening the form), the [**Show**](#show) event may fire while Access is still executing its `IOleControl::FreezeEvents(False)` call. Access does not deliver events until after that call returns, so any `RaiseEvent` call inside the **Show** handler receives an `E_FAIL` HRESULT from the host's event sink. The control appears as a blank box and does not initialize; subsequent opens of the form work correctly. This behaviour does not occur in VB6, Excel VBA, or C# WinForms hosts. A workaround for builds before BETA 498 is to place `On Error Resume Next` immediately before each `RaiseEvent` statement in the **Show** handler. The underlying `IOleControl::FreezeEvents` race condition was fixed in twinBASIC **BETA 498**.
>
> Additionally, host-specific errors with a twinBASIC **UserControl** should always be reproduced with a freshly compiled binary before investigating the control's own source code. The compiler's ActiveX code generation has been updated frequently, and a binary compiled with an old build can exhibit issues that no longer exist in the current compiler.

_Source threads: 1227298948352442469 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-04-09 to 2024-04-10_
_Reviewer note: This note should be inserted after the Show event's Syntax line (under the ### Show heading in the Events section), before the ### Terminate heading. Verify that the FreezeEvents fix landed in BETA 498 specifically -- the thread mentions this build number._

## Deployment notes

### Runtime license embedding

twinBASIC embeds ActiveX runtime licenses into compiled executables and OCX files at build time, the same way VB6 does. A control compiled with twinBASIC that uses a licensed third-party ActiveX component (such as a spreadsheet or grid control) runs correctly on a machine that has no development environment installed, provided the control's `IClassFactory2` license key is available at compile time.

If a specific control's runtime license is not embedded correctly, it is a per-control issue rather than a general twinBASIC deficiency. Report such cases with the control name and author so the embedding behavior can be investigated for that specific control.

### "Subject is not trusted for the specified Action" in VBA hosts

> [!NOTE]
> The error message "This user is not trusted for the specified operation" (English form: "Subject is not trusted for the specified Action") appearing when a twinBASIC-compiled OCX is loaded in a VBA host does **not** indicate a runtime license problem. It indicates an ActiveX trust or security restriction in the host environment.

Two known causes are:

- **Office 2024 LTSC** --- ActiveX controls are disabled by default. The host application requires a registry or policy change to re-enable them before any ActiveX control, regardless of origin, can be loaded.
- **Windows ActiveX kill bits** --- registry entries associated with a control's CLSID can block that control from instantiating in any host, independent of licensing. Inspect the kill-bit registry keys for the control's GUID if the Office ActiveX setting is not the cause.

_Source threads: 1306802204178518046 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-11-15_
_Reviewer note: Verify that twinBASIC's license-embedding behavior is consistently documented and still accurate as of the current release. The thread confirms Far Point Spread 6.0 worked; confirm the general claim still holds for the current compiler version._

## Deployment notes

### Architecture and host bitness

> [!NOTE]
> The compiled OCX must match the bitness of the host application. If the host is 32-bit (for example, Office 2010 Excel VBA) but the OCX was compiled as x64, COM registration appears to succeed but the host reports "No registered class" when it tries to use the control. Recompile the OCX targeting the same architecture as the host to resolve this. The IDE remembers the last-used target architecture setting per project to reduce the chance of building for the wrong architecture by accident.

> [!NOTE]
> A regression introduced after twinBASIC BETA 592 causes x64-compiled OCX controls to fail with an "Element not found" error when loaded in a VBA host (such as an Office Excel form). The same x64 OCX loads correctly when referenced from a twinBASIC EXE project. Until the regression is resolved, x64 OCX controls intended for use in VBA hosts should be compiled with BETA 592 or earlier. This issue is tracked in twinBASIC GitHub issue #1918.

_Source threads: 1306959748800970772 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-11-15_

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC fires **UserControl** lifecycle events in a different order than VB6 in several design-time and run-time scenarios. Code that depends on VB6's exact event sequence may need adjustment:
>
> - **Placing a UC on a form at design time** fires multiple extra **Resize** events and an unexpected **WriteProperties**/**Initialize** cycle that VB6 does not produce.
> - **Resizing a UC at design time** fires multiple **Resize** events followed by **WriteProperties**; VB6 fires a single **Resize**.
> - **Running a project** omits the **WriteProperties** that VB6 fires before **Initialize**.
> - **Closing a running form** fires no events in twinBASIC; VB6 fires **Initialize** / **ReadProperties** / **Resize** on the UC.
> - **Placing a child control on a UC with `ControlContainer = True` at design time** incorrectly resets module-level global variables and fires **Initialize** / **ReadProperties** / **Resize** / **WriteProperties** in twinBASIC; VB6 fires nothing.
> - **Moving a UC on a form at design time** fires **WriteProperties** in twinBASIC; VB6 fires nothing.
> - **Closing a form designer** fires nothing in twinBASIC; VB6 fires **WriteProperties**.
> - **Opening a form designer** fires an extra **WriteProperties** in twinBASIC that VB6 does not fire.

_Source threads: 1447301617065136159 · confidence: medium_
_Date range: 2025-12-06 to 2026-01-08_
_Reviewer note: These deviations were observed and discussed in Discord threads from December 2025 through January 2026 and described as active bugs. Verify current status against the latest twinBASIC release before publishing, as some items may have been corrected._

> [!NOTE]

Guard the call explicitly:
>
> ```tb
> Private Sub UserControl_Resize()
>     If Me.EventsFrozen = False Then RaiseEvent RefreshContents(CC)
> End Sub
> ```
>
> Additionally, **UserControl** projects that are not DPI-aware should set the project DPI-awareness option to **NONE** to avoid layout issues on high-DPI displays.

### ClipControls
{: .no_toc }

Whether child controls are clipped out of the **UserControl**'s drawing region during paint. **Boolean**, default **True**. Read-only at run time --- set at design time.

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC versions before BETA 245, setting **ClipControls** to **True** on a **UserControl** that contained a **PictureBox** could leave stale pixels after the parent form was clipped smaller and then expanded again. The **PictureBox** invalidation was skipped on the **ClipControls = True** paint path, so the control appeared not to redraw. This was fixed in BETA 245.

## docs/Reference/VB/UserControl/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1070782782210572400]

## VBA host notes

These notes apply when a twinBASIC **UserControl** is compiled as a DLL and embedded in a VBA userform (Microsoft Access, Excel, or another Office host).

### Designer type-info cache and CLSID

> [!NOTE]
> The VBA userform designer caches control metadata by CLSID. If the control's public interface changes --- new or removed properties, changed type signatures --- but the CLSID is not updated, the designer may load stale cached type information and report errors such as *User defined type not defined* for types that are correctly exported in the updated typelib.

The fix is to assign a new CLSID to the control class (and typically also a new IID and EventInterfaceId) so the VBA designer treats the updated binary as a brand-new control. After changing the CLSID, delete any existing instance of the old control from the userform and add the control again from the toolbox.

### 64-bit process teardown crash with Shell namespace objects

> [!NOTE]
> A 64-bit **UserControl** that holds Shell namespace COM objects (`IShellFolder`, `IExplorerBrowser`, and similar) may cause an access violation during process teardown in a 64-bit VBA host (Access 64-bit, Excel 64-bit). The crash originates in system DLLs such as `DUI70.dll` or `prnfldr.dll` when those DLLs are unloaded from the process before the control releases its cached Shell references in [**Terminate**](#terminate). This does not occur in 32-bit VB6 or in twinBASIC itself.

The suggested workaround is to call `LoadLibrary("shell32.dll")` in [**Initialize**](#initialize) to keep `shell32.dll` resident for the lifetime of the process, so it is not unloaded before the control's cleanup runs. In some cases additional system DLLs may be involved; if the crash persists after pinning `shell32.dll`, inspect the faulting module name in the crash report to identify any further DLLs that need pinning.

### Access-specific: Frame control conflict

> [!NOTE]
> There is a known issue in Microsoft Access where placing a **Frame** control on a VBA userform that also contains a twinBASIC ActiveX **UserControl** causes the form to fail to load or behave incorrectly. The same layout works in Excel. When diagnosing a load or crash failure that is specific to Access, reproduce the problem in Excel first to determine whether the issue is host-specific before investigating the control itself.

_Source threads: 1100160383223861259 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-04-24 to 2023-05-01_
_Reviewer note: Three related gotchas merged into one section. Finding 2 (64-bit teardown crash) is medium confidence and the LoadLibrary workaround was not confirmed to resolve the root cause in the original report --- the note reflects this. Finding 3 (Access Frame conflict) is also medium confidence. Verify the CLSID/IID change guidance against the twinBASIC attribute syntax (e.g. [COMClassId], [InterfaceId], [EventInterfaceId]) if those are documented elsewhere, and consider linking to them._

> [!NOTE]
> **ActiveX controls that do not support DEP.** twinBASIC enables Data Execution Prevention (DEP) for all projects by default. Older ActiveX controls (OCX files) that were not built with DEP support will cause a hard crash at instantiation time, often appearing as a RESYNC error or a native exception in the debug console. The workaround is to disable DEP in both places: the project settings for the affected project, and the IDE-wide setting under **Tools > IDE Options**. Changing only the project setting is not sufficient.

> [!NOTE]
> When the twinBASIC IDE is moved between monitors with different DPI settings, the window can become oversized or move off-screen with its title bar unreachable. Two recovery options are available: (1) In **Tools > IDE Options**, enable **Show real OS titlebar** --- this keeps the close button and standard OS window-management accessible at all times. (2) **Alt+F4** closes the IDE even when the custom title bar is inaccessible. Restarting the IDE after closing it this way restores normal window placement. The underlying cause is that the IDE's WebView2-based renderer does not reliably handle monitor changes mid-session.

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052956564782329896, 1074248691579359332, 1226952899154939995, 1246753119723982950, 1357029647627452486, 1353265142938206260, 1373288305504030781, 1381124721583587389, 1382782377129934920, 1390195119705034772, 1390629968291041311, 1446527244209225854, 1448412836064657622, 1449796414828712049, 1477405818444845328, 1070748344927924314, 1246536404540981381, 1376032917725380678, 1411281230078414928, 1149349187285172306, 1161458213875621939, 1161458213875621939, 1162740282769543210, 1173248550218498089, 1308582964677836851, 1454017594691420327, 1454401227721805987, 1473790364539420864, 1488446447505641584]

> [!NOTE]
> VB6 calls `SetErrorMode(SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS Or SEM_NOOPENFILEERRORBOX)` early in its startup sequence, which suppresses the OS-level modal error dialogs that Windows displays when a Win32 file API (such as `GetFileAttributesW`) targets a removable drive with no media. twinBASIC through BETA 960 does not make this call, so on Windows 8.1 and older a `GetFileAttributesW` call (or any similar API) against an empty card reader or removable drive produces a modal system dialog that the application cannot dismiss from code. Windows 11 does not exhibit this behavior. As a workaround, call `SetErrorMode` in the application's startup `Sub Main()` before any file API calls:

```tb
Private Declare Function SetErrorMode Lib "kernel32" (ByVal uMode As Long) As Long
Private Const SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS As Long = &H1
Private Const SEM_NOOPENFILEERRORBOX As Long = &H8000

Sub Main()
    SetErrorMode SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS Or SEM_NOOPENFILEERRORBOX
    ' ... rest of startup
End Sub
```

Fixed in BETA 961, which now sets the process error mode at startup to match VB6 behavior.

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052956564782329896, 1074248691579359332, 1226952899154939995, 1246753119723982950, 1357029647627452486, 1353265142938206260, 1373288305504030781, 1381124721583587389, 1382782377129934920, 1390195119705034772, 1390629968291041311, 1446527244209225854, 1448412836064657622, 1449796414828712049, 1464345375102992576, 1070748344927924314, 1246536404540981381, 1376032917725380678, 1411281230078414928, 1149349187285172306, 1161458213875621939, 1161458213875621939, 1162740282769543210, 1173248550218498089, 1308582964677836851, 1454017594691420327, 1454401227721805987, 1473790364539420864, 1488446447505641584]

## Print target customisation

A class that implements `VB.IVBPrint` can receive output from the **Print #** statement, allowing a user-defined object to act as a print target. This makes it possible to redirect the output of legacy BASIC code --- written to print to the default output destination --- to a custom receiver such as an emulated terminal or an in-memory buffer.

```tb
Class MyTerminal
    Implements VB.IVBPrint

    ' IVBPrint requires this member:
    Private Sub IVBPrint_PrintLine(ByVal Text As String)
        ' append Text to custom terminal display
    End Sub
End Class
```

Declare the variable as `VB.IVBPrint` and use it as the file-number target in **Print #**.

## Form Designer Notes

> [!NOTE]
> When an application is running inside the IDE (debug/run mode), the form designer does not prevent edits. Controls and properties remain editable on the designer surface while the debugged application is running. Avoid making designer changes during a debug session to prevent unexpected behavior.

When multiple controls are selected on a form, the control selector dropdown at the top of the property sheet filters to show only the currently selected controls rather than all controls on the form. This makes it easier to focus on a specific control within a multi-selection, for example when working with stacked or overlapping controls. When no multi-selection is active, the dropdown shows all controls on the form.

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC applications use more GDI handles than equivalent VB6 applications --- typically two to three times as many at startup. This is a known characteristic, not a leak: the handle count is stable and does not grow over time. The Windows per-process limit of 10,000 GDI handles is unlikely to be reached in normal use. Controls that keep a private device context (`CS_OWNDC`) are the primary source of the additional handles. GDI handle *leaks* --- where the count grows continuously during use --- are treated as bugs and should be reported.

## Adding legacy ActiveX OCX controls

When adding a legacy ActiveX OCX control through **Project → References**, the control may appear as checked in the list but fail to appear in the form designer toolbox. This typically indicates a broken or missing registry entry on the development machine. Two remedies are available:

1. Open the original project in VB6, remove the OCX reference, re-add it via **Project → Components**, place the control on the relevant form(s), then re-import the project files into twinBASIC.
2. Register the OCX manually: open a command prompt in the folder containing the OCX file and run `regsvr32 YourControl.ocx` (substituting the actual file name), then perform a fresh import of the VB6 source files.

_Date range: 2026-02-18 to 2026-02-27_

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1124798976047198228, 1323993818919338034, 1309222782164402307, 1507112867147812955, 1508163583022731295, 1114463574992097360]

## Adding external ActiveX controls

External ActiveX control typelibs can be added to a twinBASIC project in two ways, and the two paths produce different results.

**Via Components** --- when a typelib is added through the Components dialog (or the Toolbox's **+ More Components** button), twinBASIC wraps the control types in `ActiveXControlExtender(Of T)` and appends a `Ctl` suffix to the library name. For example, `ActiveBarLibrary` becomes `ActiveBarLibraryCtl`. The wrapped types gain extra properties and events for IDE integration, but early-bound access to the original unwrapped type is not available through this path.

**Via References** --- when the same typelib is added through the References dialog, the original library name is preserved and no wrapping is applied. Early-bound access to the original types is available.

If a typelib is added via References first and then also via Components, both the wrapped (`ActiveBarLibraryCtl`) and unwrapped (`ActiveBarLibrary`) versions are simultaneously available. Code can then use the wrapped type for `Controls.Add` calls and cast `.Object` to the unwrapped type for direct early-bound access.

> [!NOTE]
> Controls that carry the `FCONTROL` category flag in the Windows registry --- including Microsoft Common Controls (MSCOMCTL.OCX) --- appear only in the Components dialog and cannot be added through References. The dual-reference approach is not available for these controls.

_Source threads: 1052611285310775406 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2022-12-15_

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052611285310775406, 1323993818919338034, 1309222782164402307, 1507112867147812955, 1508163583022731295, 1114463574992097360]

## StdFont and StdPicture COM interfaces

The **Font** properties on VB controls and the **Picture** / **DragIcon** / **MouseIcon** / **Image** properties return objects whose runtime type is **StdFont** and **StdPicture** respectively. Both types expose a *dispinterface* as their default COM interface---**IFontDisp** for **StdFont** and **IPictureDisp** for **StdPicture**---not the dual interfaces **IFont** and **IPicture**.

> [!NOTE]
> Dispinterface members do not have fixed vtable slots. Code that assumes the **IFont** or **IPicture** vtable layout---for example by reading member offsets through `ObjPtr` arithmetic or by casting the default interface pointer directly to **IFont**/**IPicture**---will not behave correctly. To obtain **IFont** or **IPicture**, query for the interface explicitly using `CType`.

_Source threads: 1124798976047198228 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-07-01 to 2023-07-10_

## Behavioral notes

### Disabled controls and mouse events

> [!NOTE]
> When a control's **Enabled** property is **False**, the control does not consume mouse events. Mouse move and click events pass through to whatever lies beneath it in the z-order---either another control or the form itself. This matches VB6 behavior and is by design.

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052611285310775406, 1124798976047198228, 1323993818919338034, 1507112867147812955, 1508163583022731295, 1114463574992097360]

## Setting a property from code fires the control's event

Assigning a value to a control property from code raises the same event that a user interaction would raise. This matches VB6 behavior and applies to all standard VB controls:

| Control | Property | Event raised |
|---------|----------|--------------|
| **CheckBox** | `Value` | `Click` |
| **OptionButton** | `Value` | `Click` |
| **ListBox** | `Selected` | `Click` |
| **ComboBox** | `Text` | `Click` |
| **TextBox** | `Text` | `Change` |

Two patterns are in common use to suppress the unwanted event:

**Boolean flag** --- a module-level variable guards the handler body:

```tb
Private m_Updating As Boolean

Private Sub SetCheckValue(ByVal v As CheckBoxConstants)
    m_Updating = True
    Check1.Value = v
    m_Updating = False
End Sub

Private Sub Check1_Click()
    If m_Updating Then Exit Sub
    ' ... handle genuine user click
End Sub
```

**EventSink class** --- a wrapper class intercepts the event and re-raises it only when the change originated from a user interaction. This approach requires more setup but is reusable across forms.

_Source threads: 1309222782164402307 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-11-21 to 2024-11-23_

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052611285310775406, 1124798976047198228, 1323993818919338034, 1309222782164402307, 1508163583022731295, 1114463574992097360]

## Deployment notes

### UAC elevation and the application manifest

Windows applies heuristics to compiled executables to decide whether to request elevation at launch. The heuristics scan the filename and binary content for strings associated with installer packages. A compiled twinBASIC `.exe` can trigger the UAC prompt and display the UAC shield icon in Explorer even when it contains no code that requires elevated privileges and is not named `setup`, `install`, `patch`, or similar.

The fix is to add an explicit `<trustInfo>` element to the project's application manifest:

```xml
<trustInfo xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3">
  <security>
    <requestedPrivileges>
      <requestedExecutionLevel level="asInvoker" uiAccess="false" />
    </requestedPrivileges>
  </security>
</trustInfo>
```

This declaration overrides the heuristic. Without it, the default manifest contains no explicit execution level, leaving the decision to Windows. With it, the application launches without elevation and without the shield icon.

_Source threads: 1507112867147812955 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2026-05-21_
