## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052611285310775406, 1124798976047198228, 1323993818919338034, 1309222782164402307, 1507112867147812955, 1114463574992097360]

### ActiveX DLL registration and VB6 interop

When a 32-bit ActiveX DLL is built from twinBASIC it is by default registered in `HKEY_CURRENT_USER`. VB6 requires COM classes to be registered in `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE` and cannot instantiate a class registered only in `HKCU`; the attempt raises a *class not registered* error.

To make a twinBASIC ActiveX DLL instantiable from VB6:

1. Change the project setting that controls the registration target from `HKCU` to `HKLM`.
2. Run the twinBASIC IDE with elevated (administrator) privileges so that writing to `HKLM` is permitted.
3. Rebuild the DLL.

After rebuilding, the class is registered under `HKLM` and `Set oObj = New MyClass` in VB6 succeeds.

## docs/Reference/VB/index.md · new-section [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1052611285310775406, 1124798976047198228, 1323993818919338034, 1309222782164402307, 1507112867147812955, 1508163583022731295]

### 64-bit-only Win32 APIs

Windows blocks certain device-management operations when called from a 32-bit process running under WOW64. Enabling or disabling hardware devices through the SetupAPI / ConfigManager APIs, and displaying the Resources tab in a device property page, both require a native 64-bit process. VB6, which is always 32-bit, cannot call these APIs. twinBASIC's support for native 64-bit builds provides access to these operations from the VB-style development environment.

See the open-source [Device Explorer](https://github.com/fafalone/DeviceExplorer) project for a complete example.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Collection/Item.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1051396836147068999]

> [!NOTE]
> When a **Collection** object is stored as a field inside a **Type** (UDT), default property access on that field does not work correctly in twinBASIC. Code such as `this.Items(1)` or `this.Items(key)` causes a runtime error or a native access-violation exception, even though the compiler reports no error and identical code works in VBA and VB6. The workaround is to call **Item** explicitly: `this.Items.Item(1)` or `this.Items.Item(key)`. The same restriction applies to **Scripting.Dictionary** objects stored in a UDT field: use `this.Dict.Item(key)` rather than `this.Dict(key)`. A related chained-access pattern is also affected: `d.Item("root")("errNumber")` fails, while `d("root").Item("errNumber")` succeeds. The root cause is that twinBASIC treats an object stored in a UDT field as late-bound, and default-property dispatch in that context does not operate correctly.

_Source threads: 1201158504015220766 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-01-28 to 2024-06-20_

## docs/Reference/VBA/Collection/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1225415647387975751]

> [!NOTE]
> The twinBASIC **Collection** implementation uses pre-allocated internal buffers for performance. Each instance therefore occupies more memory than the equivalent VB6 **Collection**. Applications that create large numbers of small collections---for example, one collection per sprite or per record---can consume substantially more aggregate memory than expected. The planned fix will reduce per-instance overhead before v1.0. Until then, use arrays instead of collections when many instances are created or when memory use is a concern.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Constants/VbVarType.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC has no built-in `vbLongPtr` constant. Because `LongPtr` resolves to `Long` on 32-bit targets and `LongLong` on 64-bit targets, the corresponding VarType code differs by platform. The following declaration reproduces the constant using conditional compilation:
>
> ```tb
> #If Win64 Then
>     Private Declare Const vbLongPtr = &H14   ' vbLongLong (20)
> #Else
>     Private Declare Const vbLongPtr = &H3    ' vbLong (3)
> #End If
> ```
>
> Note that `VT_PTR` (&H1A) is a separate COM Variant type code, not the same as `vbLongPtr`; it is used in low-level interop scenarios such as `DispCallFunc` calls that accept a pointer-typed argument.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/CDec.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, a standalone **Decimal** variable carries the COM variant type `VT_BYREF | VT_DECIMAL` (0x400E), not plain `VT_DECIMAL` (0x000E). This differs from a **Decimal** value stored inside a **Variant**, where the `wReserved` field of the underlying `DECIMAL` struct equals `VT_DECIMAL`. Code that inspects or sets the `vt` discriminator directly---such as Win32 SAFEARRAY interop---must account for this distinction.

**Decimal arrays and SAFEARRAY interop.** A typed **Decimal** array (declared `As Decimal`) and a **Variant** array (declared `As Variant`) both have `cbElements = 16` (0x10) in their `SAFEARRAY` header, but their `fFeatures` flags differ: a **Decimal** array has `FADF_VARIANT = 0`, while a **Variant** array has `FADF_VARIANT = 0x800`. Code that distinguishes element types by inspecting `SAFEARRAY` flags must check `FADF_VARIANT` to tell a **Decimal** array apart from a **Variant** array.

On x64 builds, a **Decimal** value remains 16 bytes (matching VB6/x86 behavior), but a **Variant** is 24 bytes. These two types are not interchangeable in size on x64, and `SAFEARRAY.cbElements` will be 16 for a **Decimal** array regardless of the platform.

When calling `SafeArrayGetElement` on a SAFEARRAY typed as `VT_DECIMAL` (declared `As Decimal`), passing a **Variant** as the output argument returns **Empty** rather than the element value. To read a **Decimal** element correctly, declare a local **Decimal** variable, pass its address via `ByVal VarPtr(...)`, and then convert the result to a **Variant** with `CVar` if needed:

```tb
Private Sub SAGetDecimalElement(ByVal ipArrayAddr As LongPtr, _
                                ByVal ipIndexesAddr As LongPtr, _
                                ByRef opVariant As Variant)
    Dim myD As Decimal = 0
    SafeArrayGetElement ipArrayAddr, ipIndexesAddr, ByVal VarPtr(myD)
    opVariant = CVar(myD)
End Sub
```

Passing `ByRef Any` (which passes `VarPtr` implicitly) or `ByVal VarPtr(Variant)` both fail with a **Decimal**-typed SAFEARRAY.

_Source threads: 1367919649873858570 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-05-02 to 2025-05-03_
_Reviewer note: All four findings come from the same thread and concern Decimal SAFEARRAY interop. The VT_BYREF|VT_DECIMAL behavior (finding 1) is marked medium confidence by the extractor; fafalone indicated tB 'seems to understand a Decimal as a Decimal' but the thread did not reach a definitive conclusion on why VT_BYREF arises for standalone variables. The workaround (finding 3) is confirmed working but also medium confidence. The x64 size difference (finding 2, high confidence) and SAFEARRAY flags (finding 4) are corroborated by inspection output in the thread. Verify VT_BYREF|VT_DECIMAL behavior against the twinBASIC .twin runtime source before publishing._

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/CLngPtr.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> On 64-bit targets, `vbNullPtr` is a built-in constant equal to `CLngPtr(0)`, which has type **LongLong**. Passing it to a `Declare` function parameter typed `ByRef Long` produces a compile error because the compiler cannot coerce **LongLong** to `[ByRef] Long`. The `ByVal` modifier at the call site does not resolve this. The literal `ByVal 0` works because the untyped integer literal `0` is a **Long**. Defining a module-level constant `Const vbNullPtr As Long = 0` shadows the built-in and restores **Long** type, but this also disables any future null-pointer-passing feature that depends on the built-in constant. Extending the existing `ByRef` null-pointer syntax (already supported for UDTs) to cover primitive `ByRef` parameters was a planned improvement that had not yet been implemented at the time of writing.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/CStr.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> On Windows 8.1 and earlier, when the system regional short date format uses a dot separator (for example `dd.MM.yyyy`), **CStr** applied to a **Date** value may swap the day and month components. For example, `CStr(CDate("10.09.2025"))` returns `"09.10.2025"` instead of `"10.09.2025"`. This does not occur on Windows 10 and later, and VB6 is not affected. Use [**FormatDateTime**](../Strings/FormatDateTime) instead of **CStr** or implicit conversion when converting a **Date** to a **String** on systems that may run Windows 8.1 or earlier, as **FormatDateTime** handles regional locale settings correctly on all versions.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/CType.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1326921370591826090, 1386545607916912720, 1461920977519640657]

> [!NOTE]
> When dereferencing a raw pointer to a UDT, two techniques are equivalent:
>
> - `CType(Of T)(ptr)` where *ptr* is a **LongPtr** obtained from **VarPtr** or an API return value --- this treats the pointer as a typed reference to a *T* without copying the data.
> - Passing *ptr* **ByVal** as the argument to any **Declare** or **Sub** whose parameter is typed **As** *SomeUDT* --- the runtime dereferences the pointer at the call boundary.
>
> For single-indirection cases where the caller already has a UDT variable in scope, passing **ByRef As** *UDT* is preferred because twinBASIC allows substituting a **ByVal As LongPtr** argument at the call site when needed.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/CType.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1326921370591826090, 1459605334502150206, 1461920977519640657]

> [!NOTE]
> The pointer-reinterpretation role of **CType** applies only when the target type *T* is a **user-defined type** and the source expression is a **LongPtr**. When *T* is an **interface** type, **CType** does not dereference the pointer --- its role is limited to suppressing the TB0020 suspicious-conversion warning when assigning between interface types where the source type is not statically known to implement the target interface. Using `CType(Of ISomeInterface)(aLongPtr)` to assign a raw pointer to an interface variable will cause a linker or code-generation error. For that pattern, use [**vbaObjSetAddref**](../HiddenModule/vbaObjSetAddref) (to assign from an object pointer as returned by `ObjPtr`) or zero the destination with `PutMemPtr(VarPtr(dest), vbNullPtr)` before the assignment.

> Dim ptr As LongPtr = CType(Of HSTRING)(MakeNamespace(StrRef("StringMap"))).hStringPtr
>
> ' Correct form for beta 948 and later:
> Dim h As HSTRING = MakeNamespace(StrRef("StringMap"))
> Dim ptr As LongPtr = h.hStringPtr
> ```

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/CType.md · example

### Cryptographically secure random LongLong

The following example uses the WinRT `ICryptographicBufferStatics.GenerateRandom` method to fill a buffer with random bytes, then reads the result as a `LongLong` through a pointer-to-UDT reinterpretation. All WinRT and .NET random functions call the same OS-provided RNG internally, so this path produces cryptographically secure values without a `Declare`-based API call.

The interface declarations shown below can be replaced by the equivalent declarations from WinDevLib if that package is already referenced.

```tb
' Minimum interface declarations required (or use WinDevLib equivalents)
[InterfaceId("320B7E22-3CB0-4CDF-8663-1D28910065EB")]
Interface ICryptographicBufferStatics Extends IInspectable
    Function Compare(ByVal Buffer1 As IBuffer, ByVal Buffer2 As IBuffer) As Boolean
    Function GenerateRandom(ByVal Length As Long) As IBuffer
    ' ... remaining members omitted for brevity
End Interface

[InterfaceId("905A0FE0-BC53-11DF-8C49-001E4FC686DA")]
Interface IBuffer Extends IInspectable
    Property Get Capacity() As Long
    Property Get Length() As Long
    Property Let Length(ByVal Value As Long)
End Interface

[InterfaceId("905A0FEF-BC53-11DF-8C49-001E4FC686DA")]
Interface IBufferByteAccess Extends IUnknown
    Function Buffer() As LongPtr
End Interface

' Helper UDT for reinterpretation
Private Type tLongLong
    LongLong As LongLong
End Type

Public Function RandomLongLong() As LongLong
    ' Obtain a WinRT statics object for the buffer class (activation omitted)
    ' then reinterpret the raw buffer pointer as a tLongLong:
    RandomLongLong = CType(Of tLongLong)( _
        CType(Of IBufferByteAccess)( _
            CryptographicBufferStatics.GenerateRandom(LenB(Of LongLong)) _
        ).Buffer _
    ).LongLong
End Function
```

`CType(Of IBufferByteAccess)(...)` performs an interface-query cast on the `IBuffer` object returned by `GenerateRandom`. `CType(Of tLongLong)(ptr)` then reinterprets the raw byte-pointer as the UDT, reading the eight bytes in place without copying them.

_Source threads: 1310567792575250442 · confidence: medium_
_Date range: 2024-11-25 to 2024-11-27_
_Reviewer note: The activation step for ICryptographicBufferStatics (obtaining the WinRT statics object) is omitted from the example for brevity. Verify the complete working pattern against the GenerateRandom.twinproj attachment referenced in the thread before publishing. The one-liner form in the thread compresses both CType calls into a single expression; the expanded form here may be clearer for readers._

## docs/Reference/VBA/Conversion/index.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC is introducing **DCast(Of T)** (the name may change before release), a direct bit-copy cast that copies the raw bits of a value into the target type without interpreting sign or performing range checks. This differs from the standard C-prefix functions --- [**CInt**](CInt), [**CLng**](CLng), and so on --- which perform numeric conversion and raise a run-time error when the source value is out of the target type's range. For example, `DCast(Of Integer)(&hffff&)` yields `-1` instead of an overflow error. **DCast(Of T)** is a twinBASIC-specific addition with no VBA equivalent.

## docs/Reference/VBA/DateTime/TimeSerial.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> The **Date** type stores values as an OLE Automation **Double** --- the integer part counts days from 1899-12-30, the fractional part encodes the time of day. The **Double** has enough precision to represent milliseconds (roughly 1.157 × 10⁻⁸ of a day per millisecond), but the OLE date-parsing layer --- including **TimeSerial**, **Hour**, **Minute**, and **Second** --- operates on the `UDATE` structure, which has no milliseconds field. Sub-second values are silently discarded whenever a **Date** value passes through any of these functions. There is no **TimeSerial** equivalent that accepts a milliseconds argument, and no **VBA.Millisecond** extraction function. A raw arithmetic offset into the **Double** can survive a round-trip as long as it never passes through an OLE date-parsing function, but this is not a supported pattern.

_Source threads: 1304492203212800051 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-11-08 to 2024-11-15_

## docs/Reference/VBA/ErrObject/Raise.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1119039863681990728, 1208041491641925692, 1254068987453505627, 1295449857787695217]

> [!NOTE]
> **Err.Raise inside a tB Standard DLL does not propagate to a VB6 caller.** Calling **Raise** from within a tB Standard DLL function does not populate the calling VB6 program's `Err` object. Instead, twinBASIC displays an error message box with the error number and description. [**ReturnHResult**](ReturnHResult) also has no effect across a plain DLL boundary.
>
> The correct mechanism for returning an error status to a VB6 caller is `SetLastError` (kernel32) on the tB side, then reading [**Err.LastDllError**](LastDllError) on the VB6 side immediately after the call. This does not raise a trappable error --- `On Error GoTo` will not fire; the caller must check the value explicitly.
>
> For full COM error propagation (so that `Err.Raise` and `On Error` work on both sides), expose the functionality through a COM server (ActiveX DLL class) rather than through plain `Declare`-based DLL entry points.

> [!NOTE]

In VB6, shell extensions such as context menu handlers (`IContextMenu`) required v-table manipulation to return arbitrary HRESULTs from interface methods, because VB6 had no direct mechanism for this. ## docs/Reference/VBA/HiddenModule/GetMem4.md · example

This example reads the real Windows version numbers directly from `KUSER_SHARED_DATA`, the kernel-mapped region that Windows always places at user-mode address `0x7FFE0000` for both 32-bit and 64-bit processes. The fields at offsets `0x260` (build number), `0x26C` (major version), and `0x270` (minor version) report the actual OS version, bypassing the compatibility shims applied by `GetVersionEx` and related APIs.

```tb
Dim dwMajor As Long
Dim dwMinor As Long
Dim dwBuild As Long
GetMem4 &H7FFE026C, dwMajor
GetMem4 &H7FFE0270, dwMinor
GetMem4 &H7FFE0260, dwBuild
Debug.Print "Windows " & dwMajor & "." & dwMinor & " Build " & dwBuild
```

The fixed address `0x7FFE0000` is documented by Microsoft and stable across x86 and x64 processes, including Large Address Aware (LAA) builds.

_Source threads: 1220275909311856650 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-03-21_

## docs/Reference/VBA/HiddenModule/PutMem4.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> Constructing a **LongLong** from two **Long** values by shifting and combining them with bitwise arithmetic can produce overflow errors. Because **LongLong** is a signed type, shifting a value into the high 32 bits may set the sign bit and cause an overflow. The safe pattern is to assign the low part directly and write the high part with **PutMem4**:
>
> ```tb
> Dim Value As LongLong
> Value = LowPart
> PutMem4 VarPtr(Value) + 4, HighPart
> ```
>
> Alternatively, copy all eight bytes in one call using [**vbaCopyBytes**](vbaCopyBytes), or use a **LARGE_INTEGER**-style UDT and [**CType**](../../Conversion/CType) if the Windows Development Library is referenced.

## docs/Reference/VBA/HiddenModule/vbaAryMove.md · example

### Example

This example overlays a twinBASIC array over an external (non-SAFEARRAY) memory block --- for instance, pixel data returned by a `IWICBitmapLock.GetDataPointer` call --- so that standard array syntax (`UBound`, indexing, `For Each`) can be used over the raw memory without copying it.

```tb
' SAFEARRAY descriptor built by hand for a Byte array.
Private Type SAFEARRAY1D
    cDims     As Integer
    fFeatures As Integer   ' Set FADF_AUTO (&H21) to prevent the runtime
                           ' from freeing the external memory on scope exit.
    cbElements As Long
    cLocks     As Long
    pvData     As LongPtr
    cElements  As Long
    lLBound    As Long
End Type

Sub OverlayArray(ByVal pData As LongPtr, ByVal nBytes As Long)
    Dim tSA    As SAFEARRAY1D
    Dim bPixels() As Byte

    tSA.cDims     = 1
    tSA.fFeatures = &H21   ' FADF_AUTO -- do not free pvData on cleanup
    tSA.cbElements = 1
    tSA.cElements  = nBytes
    tSA.pvData     = pData

    ' Point bPixels at the manually built descriptor.
    CopyMemory ByVal VarPtr(bPixels), VarPtr(tSA), LenB(Of LongPtr)

    ' bPixels now indexes the external block directly.
    Debug.Print "First byte: "; bPixels(0)

    ' Move semantics: transfer ownership and leave the source empty.
    Dim bDest() As Byte
    vbaAryMove bDest, bPixels
End Sub
```

The `FADF_AUTO` flag prevents the runtime from freeing `pvData` when `bPixels` goes out of scope, so the external memory is not freed by the array cleanup. **vbaAryMove** transfers the descriptor from `bPixels` to `bDest` in O(1) time and leaves `bPixels` unallocated.

_Source threads: 1210842540043931699 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-02-24 to 2024-02-26_
_Reviewer note: The SAFEARRAY1D UDT layout and FADF_AUTO value should be verified against the Windows SDK SAFEARRAY definition. The CopyMemory approach and VarPtr(bPixels) usage should be confirmed against twinBASIC behavior for array variables._

## docs/Reference/VBA/HiddenModule/vbaCopyBytes.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1390391690845618388]

> [!WARNING]
> Copying a **SAFEARRAY** descriptor pointer with **vbaCopyBytes** can cause the same array to be destroyed twice: once when the local variable that received the copy goes out of scope, and once by whatever else holds the original pointer. This double-free corrupts the heap. To transfer ownership of an array's storage safely, use [vbaAryMove](vbaAryMove), which has move semantics: it releases any existing destination array, moves the source pointer, and leaves the source in the unallocated state. The double-free risk does not apply when the manually constructed **SAFEARRAY** descriptor carries the `FADF_AUTO` feature flag, which tells the runtime not to free the backing memory on destruction.

> BindArray b1, VarPtr(sa1), Len(Of LongPtr)

## docs/Reference/VBA/HiddenModule/vbaRefVarAry.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1382015106380075078]

> [!NOTE]

' Destructuring on the left:
Dim x As Variant, y As Variant
Array(x, y) = SomeFunction()

Dim vals As Variant

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/Array.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1352615518212980827, 1165935542375030815, 1340649614956691476]

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC (BETA 587 and later), `Array()` is a generic intrinsic handled entirely by the compiler. The element subtype is inferred from the assignment target or the parameter type of the receiving procedure, so `Dim myLongs() As Long = Array(1, 2, 3)` produces a native `Long` array with no **Variant** involved. When inference is not possible, the explicit form `Array(Of Long)(1, 2, 3)` supplies the subtype directly. If neither inference nor an explicit subtype is provided, the subtype defaults to **Variant**, preserving classic VBx behavior.
>
> Dynamic array variables can also be initialized directly on the `Dim` line inside a procedure. Field initializers at class or module level (e.g. `Private myArray() As Long = Array(1, 2, 3)`) are not yet supported and can cause IDE crashes --- initialize module-level arrays in the constructor instead.
>
> The compiler enforces strict subtype compatibility: assigning `Array(1, 2, 3)` to a `Long()` variable works (integer literals are widened), but specifying an incompatible explicit subtype (e.g. `Array(Of Integer)(...)` when the target is `Long()`) is a compile error even if the values would fit at run time.

> [!NOTE]

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/IsArrayInitialized.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> `Array()` called with no arguments returns an initialized but empty array --- `IsArrayInitialized(Array())` returns **True**. This is by design: **IsArrayInitialized** tests whether a SAFEARRAY structure exists, not whether the array contains any elements. A `Dim a() As Long` declaration leaves the variable uninitialized (**False**), while `Array()` allocates an empty SAFEARRAY (**True**).
>
> To test whether an initialized array actually contains elements, check the bounds after confirming initialization: `If IsArrayInitialized(arr) AndAlso LBound(arr) <= UBound(arr) Then`. Calling **LBound** or **UBound** on an uninitialized array raises a run-time error, so the **IsArrayInitialized** guard must come first. A common pattern for lazy initialization is `If Not IsArrayInitialized(myArray) Then myArray = Split(vbNullString)`, which ensures subsequent **LBound** / **UBound** calls are safe even when the array holds no elements.

_Date range: 2023-11-16 to 2023-11-17_

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/IsMissing.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1114958537970421911, 1297220598014935091]

> [!NOTE]
> When an **Optional Variant** parameter is omitted, its internal representation is `VarType = vbError` with the value `CVErr(448)` (`DISP_E_PARAMNOTFOUND`). **IsMissing** checks both the error code and an additional internal flag; passing `CVErr(448)` directly does not satisfy **IsMissing**, which still returns **False** for it.
>
> To propagate an unpassed state through a wrapper function, declare the wrapper with its own **Optional Variant** parameter and assign the inner parameter directly --- for example, `GetMissingValue = IgnoreIt`. This preserves the internal flag so **IsMissing** returns **True** in the callee. There is no built-in syntax to forward an unpassed optional argument directly from a call site.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/RGB.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> Color properties such as `BackColor` and `ForeColor` store values in BGR byte order (blue in the low byte, red in the high byte of the three-byte value), the same convention used by VB6 and VBA. The **RGB** function produces values in this format automatically --- `RGB(255, 0, 0)` returns the correct representation of red. When entering a color as a hex literal, the bytes must follow BGR order: the hex constant `&H0000FF` represents red (blue=0, green=0, red=255), not blue. The [**ColorConstants**](../../../Packages/VBRUN/Constants/ColorConstants) enumeration provides named constants in the correct byte order.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/StrPtr.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1177269307625984082, 1437514645354315888]

> [!NOTE]
> In programs that override the default entry point --- kernel-mode drivers or user-mode programs with a custom `wWinMain` --- the normal twinBASIC startup routine that initializes module-level variables does not run. As a result, **StrPtr** on a module-level **String** variable returns 0 in this context, even when the declaration appears correct. Passing a zero pointer to a native API such as `RtlInitUnicodeString` causes an access violation (or a bluescreen in a driver).
>
> Two workarounds are available:
>
> - Declare the string with **Const** instead of **Dim**.
> - Assign an explicitly initialized value using a `[ConstantFoldable]` helper before calling **StrPtr**:
>
> ```tb
> [IgnoreWarnings(TB0018)]
> [ConstantFoldable]
> Public Function CFLoopback(sIn As String) As String
>     Return StrConv(sIn, 0)
> End Function
>
> ' Assign before use:
> myModuleString = CFLoopback(myModuleString)
> Dim ptr As LongPtr: ptr = StrPtr(myModuleString)
> ```
>
> This issue is separate from the SAFEARRAY initialization problem that affects module-level arrays in the same scenario (see [**VarPtr**](VarPtr)).

_Source threads: 1378419698642845818 · confidence: medium_
_Date range: 2025-05-31 to 2025-06-27_

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/StrPtr.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1378419698642845818, 1437514645354315888]

> [!NOTE]
> An uninitialized **String** variable holds a null pointer and occupies only the pointer itself---4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 bytes on 64-bit. Assigning `""` allocates a BSTR with a 4-byte length prefix (set to zero) and a 2-byte null terminator, so the pointer becomes non-zero and 6 additional bytes are consumed. Assigning **vbNullString** resets the pointer to null, identical to an uninitialized variable, and is the correct value to pass to Win32 APIs that distinguish a null string pointer from a zero-length string.

> [!WARNING]
> Passing `StrPtr(s)` directly to a COM callback interface is unsafe. The pointer is valid only while the **String** variable is alive and unmodified; the runtime may relocate the string before the callback consumes the value, leaving a dangling pointer. When a callback interface requires a stable wide-string pointer (`LPWSTR`), allocate a COM-owned buffer with `CoTaskMemAlloc`, copy the string content into it, and pass that pointer instead.

> [!NOTE]

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/UBound.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1152604048076320778, 1321435629917044847]

> [!NOTE]
> Calling **UBound** on a dynamic array that has been declared but never assigned (for example, `Dim s() As String` with no subsequent `ReDim`) throws Run-time error 9 (Subscript out of range). This matches VB6 behavior. A distinct case is an array that has been initialized but contains no elements --- for example, one produced by `s = Array()` --- where `UBound(s)` returns -1 and `LBound(s)` returns 0, signaling an empty array. With `Option Base 1` in effect, `Array()` yields `LBound = 1, UBound = 0`. Use [IsArrayInitialized](IsArrayInitialized) to distinguish the uninitialized case before calling **UBound**.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/VarPtr.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1058358947989430332, 1110672289848103023, 1331191929374904461, 1378434923018453136, 1468855447048945847, 1136660342739566635, 1210842540043931699, 1227643424010670222, 1329056650455416852, 1458492001610760376, 1464634730321543168]

> [!NOTE]
> When an array is received as a `ByRef Variant` parameter, calling `VarPtr` on an element of that array does not return the address of the underlying array data. The Variant wrapper introduces an indirection that causes the result to be incorrect for low-level memory operations such as `RtlMoveMemory` / `CopyMemory`. This behavior is the same in VBA and twinBASIC.
>
> Two workarounds are available:
>
> - Assign the Variant parameter to a typed local array first, then call `VarPtr` on the local element. This copies the data but gives a correct address: `Dim tmpArr() As Integer : tmpArr = iopArray : VarPtr(tmpArr(0))`.
> - Declare the parameter as a typed array instead of `Variant` (e.g. `ByRef iopArray() As Integer`). This avoids the Variant boxing entirely and `VarPtr(iopArray(0))` returns the correct address.
>
> If the array itself holds `Variant` elements (rather than a typed array boxed inside a Variant), `VarPtr` on an element works correctly.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/VarPtr.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1058358947989430332, 1110672289848103023, 1214539306711130142, 1331191929374904461, 1468855447048945847, 1136660342739566635, 1210842540043931699, 1227643424010670222, 1329056650455416852, 1458492001610760376, 1464634730321543168]

> [!NOTE]
> In programs that override the default entry point --- kernel-mode drivers or user-mode programs with a custom `wWinMain` --- the normal twinBASIC startup routine that initializes global variables does not run. twinBASIC arrays are SAFEARRAYs and require that initialization; a module-level array declaration such as `Private Callbacks(1) As FLT_OPERATION_REGISTRATION` is uninitialized in this context. Calling **VarPtr** on an element of an uninitialized SAFEARRAY causes an immediate crash or bluescreen.
>
> The workaround is to embed the array inside a UDT:
>
> ```tb
> Private Type CallbackSet
>     Arr(1) As FLT_OPERATION_REGISTRATION
> End Type
> Private CB As CallbackSet
>
> ' Safe: Arr inside a UDT is a C-style array, not a SAFEARRAY.
> Dim p As LongPtr: p = VarPtr(CB.Arr(0))
> ```
>
> Arrays declared inside a UDT use C-style (fixed) storage and do not require the startup initialization. **VarPtr** on an element of a UDT-embedded array is safe in custom-entry-point programs.
>
> Module-level **String** variables are subject to a related issue (see [**StrPtr**](StrPtr)).

Code that relies on the returned address pointing directly into array memory --- for example, `vbaCopyBytes` reads based on `VarPtr` --- produces incorrect results in twinBASIC. This difference may be addressed in a future compiler update.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Information/VarPtr.md · example

This example swaps two typed arrays without copying their contents by exchanging the underlying **SAFEARRAY** pointers.

```tb
Sub Swap(Of T)(ByRef a() As T, ByRef b() As T)
    SwapPtr ByVal VarPtr(a), ByVal VarPtr(b)
End Sub

Sub SwapPtr(ByRef a As LongPtr, ByRef b As LongPtr)
    Dim temp As LongPtr = a
    a = b
    b = temp
End Sub
```

Passing `VarPtr(a)` by value to a `ByRef LongPtr` parameter causes the caller to write through the address rather than copy it, so the two **SAFEARRAY** pointers are exchanged without touching any element data. This pattern is valid in twinBASIC but does not work in VB6 due to that compiler's stricter type-mismatch rules.

_Source threads: 1464634730321543168 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2026-01-27_

In twinBASIC the same call raises a run-time error instead. To test whether a control-array element is loaded, guard the index with `LBound` / `UBound` and then probe the element's **Name** property inside an `On Error Resume Next` block:
>
> ```tb
> Dim bLoaded As Boolean
> If Index >= ControlArray.LBound And Index <= ControlArray.UBound Then
>     Dim sName As String
>     On Error Resume Next
>     sName = ControlArray(Index).Name
>     bLoaded = (Err.Number = 0) And (Len(sName) > 0)
>     On Error GoTo 0
> End If
> ```

## docs/Reference/VBA/Interaction/CallByName.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1219752937207627898, 1167758561854631986]

### Array-argument variant

`CallByName` is declared internally as alias `#9` of the `<interaction>` built-in library. Because twinBASIC exposes this alias, a second entry point can be declared that replaces the `ParamArray` with a plain array parameter, letting a pre-built argument array be passed directly:

```tb
[PreserveSig(False), UseGetLastError(False), DLLStackCheck(False)]
Public DeclareWide PtrSafe Function CallByNameArray Lib "<interaction>" Alias "#9" _
    (ByVal Object As Object, ByVal ProcName As String, _
     ByVal CallType As VbCallType, Args() As Variant) As Variant
```

With this declaration, a caller can pass any `Variant` array to `CallByNameArray` without wrapping it in a `ParamArray` construction.

_Source threads: 1270441607023296522 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2024-08-06 to 2024-08-08_
_Reviewer note: Confirmed by Wayne Phillips (twinBASIC maintainer). Verify that the alias number `#9` is stable before publishing._

> [!NOTE]
> In VBA, calling **DoEvents** inside a tight loop is a common way to keep the IDE responsive to Pause and Stop commands. This does not apply in twinBASIC. Because the twinBASIC IDE runs in a separate process from the executing code, **DoEvents** has no effect on whether the IDE's Pause and End/Stop controls respond during a long-running loop. If those controls stop responding, use the IDE's **Restart** button, which terminates the running project even when Pause and Stop are unresponsive.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Interaction/DoEvents.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1054036272546582609]

> [!NOTE]
> When a loop containing **DoEvents** is running and the user closes a form by clicking its close button, **DoEvents** processes the close/unload sequence before returning. If the loop then accesses a member of that form---such as reading a control's property---without first checking that the form is still loaded, the runtime silently creates a new invisible instance of the form. Because the process cannot terminate while loaded forms exist, this invisible instance prevents the application from exiting. The fix is to check that the form is still loaded before accessing any of its members after **DoEvents** returns. This behavior is consistent with VB6 and is not a twinBASIC-specific bug; see the **Form** class for a fuller description of this silent-reload mechanism.

> [!NOTE]
> When **MsgBox** is called from code running inside an ActiveX DLL project, the message box has no owner window and belongs to the desktop. It can appear behind the host application's window, and the host process is not blocked in the expected way. The workaround is to use the `MessageBoxIndirectW` Win32 API instead, passing the host application's window handle as the *hwndOwner* parameter. The same issue applies to modal forms shown from a DLL: call `SetWindowLongPtrW` with index `GWLP_HWNDOWNER` (-8) to assign the host's window handle as the owner before calling `Form.Show vbModal`, then call `EnableWindow` on the owner to block input to it while the modal form is displayed.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Interaction/MsgBox.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1348696576104595516]

> [!NOTE]
> **MsgBox** is modal --- it blocks the calling thread until the user dismisses the dialog. To display a message box without halting execution, create a worker thread with `CreateThread` (from the Windows Development Library for twinBASIC, WinDevLib) whose thread procedure calls `MsgBox` independently. The calling thread continues while the dialog is visible.
>
> The general pattern:
> 1. Allocate a structure (with `CoTaskMemAlloc`) that holds the message text, title, and button style.
> 2. Pass its address to `CreateThread` via `AddressOf`, pointing to the thread procedure.
> 3. In the thread procedure, call `MsgBox`, then free any BSTR strings with `SysFreeString` and the allocation with `CoTaskMemFree`. (`CoTaskMemAlloc`/`CoTaskMemFree` and `SysAllocString`/`SysFreeString` are separate allocator pairs; each allocation must be freed with its matching deallocator.)
> 4. Track the thread handle so it can be waited on and closed when the form or application unloads.
>
> For non-interactive notifications, a Windows tray notification is non-blocking by design and requires no extra thread.

_Source threads: 1487361538783449098 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2026-03-28 to 2026-03-29_

## docs/Reference/VBA/Math/Rnd.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> **Rnd** and [**Randomize**](Randomize) use the same algorithm as the VB6 runtime (MSVBM60.dll) and produce identical sequences for the same seed. Calling `Randomize 1` alone does not guarantee a repeatable sequence because **Randomize** incorporates the system timer into the seed. To obtain a fully deterministic sequence that matches VB6 behaviour, call `Rnd -1` immediately before `Randomize <seed>` --- the negative argument resets the generator to a fixed internal state before seeding.

> [!NOTE]
> In twinBASIC, **LenB(** *varname* **)** (variable-argument form) is not accepted as a constant expression and cannot be used in an array dimension. To size a byte array from a UDT at compile time, use the type-generic form **LenB(Of** *T* **)** with no variable argument:
>
> ```tb
> Type T_ArtDmx
>     ' ... members
> End Type
>
> ' Correct: type-generic form is a compile-time constant
> Dim buf(0 To LenB(Of T_ArtDmx) - 1) As Byte
>
> ' Incorrect: variable form is not a constant expression
> ' Dim sndDmx As T_ArtDmx
> ' Dim buf(0 To LenB(sndDmx) - 1) As Byte   ' compile error
> ```
>
> The type-generic **LenB(Of** *T* **)** syntax is the preferred idiom for UDT-based array sizing regardless of context. (This restriction was introduced before BETA 395 and remains the correct approach.)

## docs/Reference/VBA/Strings/Len.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1109858640229314692, 1110672289848103023, 1153698825735778465, 1124334933868036223, 1510209446012391424, 1195546112459821176]

> [!NOTE]
>
> In twinBASIC x64 builds, `Len()` and `LenB()` return different values for UDTs whose members are pointer-sized or otherwise architecture-dependent. `Len()` returns a character or element count that does not reflect the actual byte footprint on x64, while `LenB()` returns the correct byte size. Code ported from VB6 or 32-bit twinBASIC that passes `Len()` as a byte count to `CopyMemory` or uses it to size a buffer with `ReDim` will silently allocate the wrong amount of memory on x64. Always use `LenB()` when the intent is to obtain the byte size of a UDT for memory operations. When dimensioning a byte array to hold a UDT for `CopyMemory`, subtract 1 from the result because array indices are zero-based:
>
> ```tb
ReDim arr(LenB(udt) - 1)
```

> #Else

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC extends **LenB** with a generic type-argument form: **LenB(Of** *TypeName***)**. This resolves to the byte size of the named type without requiring a declared variable of that type. This is the idiomatic substitute for a `vbPtrSize` constant when passing the pointer size to memory-copy routines. The same generic form is available for **Len**. Dim sa As SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES

## docs/Reference/VBA/Strings/StrComp.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
>
> twinBASIC also exposes a `StrCmp` function (note: no trailing 'p') declared as an alias for the Windows `shlwapi` export `StrCmpW`. That function applies the current locale's collation rules, not binary (Unicode ordinal) order. The results can therefore differ from the built-in **StrComp** with `vbBinaryCompare`: for example, in most Windows locales `StrCmp("a", "A")` returns -1 (lowercase `a` sorts before uppercase `A` in locale order), which is the opposite of the ordinal result. For ordinal comparisons equivalent to `StrComp(s1, s2, vbBinaryCompare)`, use the **StrComp** function or the Win32 `CompareStringOrdinal` API (kernel32). The built-in comparison operators (`<`, `>`, `=`) use `VarBstrCmp` internally, not `StrCmpW`.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Strings/StrConv.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1467483458153746625, 1125359845936205844, 1439596445899554956]

> [!NOTE]
> The twinBASIC IDE editor (Monaco) treats all files under `ProjectFolderResources` as UTF-8. For `.bas` and `.cls` source files the IDE automatically converts between ANSI on disk and Unicode in the editor, but no such conversion applies to resource files -- the IDE has no way to determine their encoding. If a resource file is saved in ANSI encoding and contains characters outside ASCII (such as accented characters), those characters display as replacement characters (`�`) when the file is opened in the IDE. The file may still behave correctly at runtime if the program reads it as raw bytes and interprets them as ANSI -- the corruption is a display issue in the IDE, not a runtime issue.
>
> The correct approach for resource files with non-ASCII characters is to save them in UTF-8 encoding. When loading the text at runtime, use **StrConv** with **vbFromUTF8** to convert the UTF-8 byte data to a Unicode string:
>
> ```tb
> Dim utf8Bytes() As Byte
> Open App.Path & "\translations.txt" For Binary As #1
> ReDim utf8Bytes(LOF(1) - 1)
> Get #1, , utf8Bytes
> Close #1
> Dim s As String
> s = StrConv(utf8Bytes, vbFromUTF8)
> ```

## docs/Reference/VBA/Strings/StrConv.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1450476331052568708, 1125359845936205844, 1439596445899554956]

> [!NOTE]
> twinBASIC adds two conversion constants not present in standard VBA: **vbUTF8** (256) converts a twinBASIC **String** (UTF-16) to a **Byte** array containing the UTF-8 representation; **vbFromUTF8** (512) converts a **Byte** array containing UTF-8 bytes to a twinBASIC **String**. These constants are part of the [**VbStrConv**](../Constants/VbStrConv) enumeration. They cannot be combined with the Unicode-conversion constants **vbUnicode** or **vbFromUnicode**.

To convert a raw memory buffer containing ASCII or UTF-8 bytes to a **String**, copy the bytes into a **Byte** array first, then pass the array to **StrConv** with **vbFromUTF8**:

```tb
Dim b() As Byte
ReDim b(length - 1)
CopyMemory b(0), ByVal address, length
Dim s As String = StrConv(b, vbFromUTF8)
```

Alternatively, the Win32 `MultiByteToWideChar` API performs the same conversion without the intermediate copy step. **StrConv** calls `MultiByteToWideChar` internally.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Strings/StrConv.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1450476331052568708, 1467483458153746625, 1439596445899554956]

> [!NOTE]
> `StrConv` returns a **Variant**, not a **String**. When passing the result directly to an overloaded function or a `Declare` that accepts both `LongPtr` and `String` parameters, the compiler cannot resolve the call because a **Variant** is assignable to either. Wrap the call with `CStr(StrConv(...))` or `CType(Of String)(StrConv(...))` to force the **String** interpretation. Both forms coerce the **Variant** to **String** without making an extra copy of the underlying character buffer --- `StrPtr` returns the same value either way.

## docs/Reference/VBA/Strings/index.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> The `$`-suffixed and unsuffixed forms of a string function return different underlying types---**String** vs. **Variant**---which matters in two situations. First, `VarPtr` applied to the return value points at different data: for a **String** result it points at the BSTR header; for a **Variant** result it points at a **VARIANT** descriptor. Second, when the return value is passed to a parameter declared `As Any`, the runtime sees a different type tag depending on which form was called. Prefer the `$` form when a **String** is required to avoid ambiguity.

## docs/Reference/VBA/index.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
>
> When a **Variant** variable receives a value from a PROPVARIANT-based COM API (such as Windows Shell property stores or `IPropertyStore`), it may end up holding a variant type that the **VARIANT** structure does not support --- for example `VT_FILETIME` (type `64`, `0x40`). When twinBASIC subsequently assigns a new value to that variable, it calls `VariantClear` internally to release the previous value. `VariantClear` is not designed to handle PROPVARIANT-extended types and returns a failed HRESULT; twinBASIC (mirroring classic VBx behavior) ignores this error and forcibly overwrites the variant type field with `VT_EMPTY` before proceeding. Any resources held by the PROPVARIANT type are not correctly released. The correct practice is to call `PropVariantClear` (via a `Declare` or a thin wrapper) manually before reassigning a **Variant** that may have been populated by a PROPVARIANT-based API.

## docs/Reference/VBRUN/PropertyBag/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1061585833238462494]

> [!NOTE]
> Two behavioral discrepancies between twinBASIC's standalone **PropertyBag** and the host-supplied property bag passed to a **UserControl**'s `ReadProperties`/`WriteProperties` events were identified and fixed in twinBASIC BETA 203:
>
> - **`Nothing` default ignored.** When `WriteProperty` stored `Nothing` for a key, a subsequent `ReadProperty` for that key returned `Nothing` even when a non-`Nothing` default value was supplied as the second argument. The VB6 UserControl property bag uses the default value as a fallback when the stored value is `Nothing`; twinBASIC's implementation did not replicate this. Affected properties backed by object references (such as `StdFont`/`IFont` font objects) could come back as `Nothing` unexpectedly.
>
> - **Duplicate keys return the first value, not the last.** When `WriteProperty` was called multiple times for the same key, `ReadProperty` returned the value from the *first* call rather than the most recent one, because all values were appended internally. For example, writing `Nothing` then `123` under the key `"FontDetails"` resulted in `ReadProperty` returning `Nothing`. The VB6 UserControl property bag returns the value from the last `WriteProperty` call for a given key.
>
> Both discrepancies affect code that persists `UserControl` properties through a standalone **PropertyBag** (as opposed to the host-supplied bag). After BETA 203 the standalone bag behaves consistently with the host-supplied one.

## docs/Reference/WebView2/WebView2/EnvironmentOptions.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1491515655646609439]

> [!NOTE]
> When the twinBASIC IDE is installed in a location that requires elevated permissions --- such as `C:\Program Files\twinBASIC` --- the WebView2 control attempts to create its temporary data folder beside the IDE executable and silently fails because that directory is not writable. The [**Ready**](.#ready) event never fires in the IDE debugger (the [**Error**](.#error) event fires instead, or no event fires at all), so any code placed in the **Ready** handler is unreachable during a debug run. Compiled executables are unaffected because they run from a different location. To avoid this:
>
> - Run the IDE as Administrator, or
> - Install the IDE in a writable location (e.g. `C:\twinBASIC`), or
> - Set **UserDataFolder** to an explicit writable path in the control's [**Create**](.#create) event (see below).

Set **UserDataFolder** in the [**Create**](.#create) event --- not the **Load** event, which fires too late for environment configuration. A subfolder under the system temporary directory is a common choice:

```tb
Private Sub WebView21_Create()
    WebView21.EnvironmentOptions.UserDataFolder = _
        Environ$("APPDATA") & "\MyApp\WebView2\"
End Sub
```

> [!NOTE]
> `Environ$("TEMP")` and `Environ$("TMP")` are not guaranteed to be defined on all systems --- Terminal Server sessions and some locked-down environments may leave them empty. `Environ$("APPDATA")` is more reliably present, or use the Win32 API `GetTempPathA` for a robust fallback.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **IDE installed in a protected folder.** When the twinBASIC IDE is extracted to a protected directory such as `C:\Program Files\`, the WebView2 runtime cannot create its `UserDataFolder` at design time. A form containing a **WebView2** control will stall at approximately 20% loading and report an error from `webview2.twin`. The same symptom can occur when a `UserDataFolder` from a previous build exists but is no longer accessible.

Alternatively, set `UserDataFolder` to a writable path in the [**Create**](.#create) event before the environment is built. Removing the WebView2 package reference allows the form to open for design without triggering this issue.

### DocumentURL
{: .no_toc }

The current document's URL. **String**. Reading returns the live URL after every navigation; assigning is equivalent to calling [**Navigate**](#navigate). The design-time default is `https://www.twinbasic.com`, used as the auto-navigation target when [**Ready**](#ready) fires.

Place all initial navigation in the **Ready** event handler instead:
>
> ```tb
> ' CORRECT: navigate after the control is ready
> Private Sub WebView21_Ready()
>     WebView21.DocumentURL = "https://www.twinbasic.com"
> End Sub
> ```

## docs/Reference/WebView2/WebView2/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1223626230419558470, 1323659799698866246, 1399977413227581491, 1469353831891468360, 1328426844512452648, 1381129747437981766, 1454017594691420327, 1468562829949796527]

> [!NOTE]
> The *UseDeferredInvoke* parameter presents a trade-off unique to twinBASIC. With **True**, JavaScript calls into the host object are dispatched through the WNDPROC message pump, so it is safe to call back into **WebView2** methods from within the callback --- but the page receives no return value from the call. With **False** (the default), the page can receive return values, but calling **WebView2** methods from inside the callback carries reentrancy risks. Use **True** when the callback needs to manipulate the control; use **False** when the callback must return data to the JavaScript caller.

## docs/Reference/WinNativeCommonCtls/ProgressBar.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1200896677041672293]

> [!NOTE]
> The legacy `MSComctlLib.ProgressBar` ActiveX control requires a design-time license to use at design time in the twinBASIC IDE. Registering `MSCOMCTL.OCX` on the system enables runtime use only. The design-time license is normally installed by a full VB6 installation. As a lighter alternative, the VB6 distribution CD contains `.srg` files with the necessary registry entries: open the `.srg` file in a text editor, add `REGEDIT4` as the very first line, save the file with a `.reg` extension, then double-click it to merge the keys. The **WinNativeCommonCtls ProgressBar** does not use ActiveX and is 64-bit compatible; it is the recommended choice for new projects and for VB6 migrations.

When adding the WinNativeCommonCtls package (or VBCCR) to an imported VB6 project produces errors inside the package's own files --- such as unresolved constants like `vbOLEDropNone` --- a reliable workaround is to start fresh: create a new empty twinBASIC project, add the target package, delete the default Form1 to avoid name conflicts, then use the import feature to bring all files in from the original project.

## docs/Reference/WinNativeCommonCtls/Slider.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1110808982894956624, 1110808982894956624, 1270084097875640510, 1499890176833490994]

> [!NOTE]
> Calling a blocking COM method (such as `IMFMediaEngineEx.SetVolume` from the Windows Media Foundation API) from a **Scroll** or **MouseMove** event handler can cause the UI to freeze permanently --- the COM call never returns, video stops, and audio continues. The same COM call made from a **CommandButton** click or a [**Timer**](../VB/Timer/) event does not trigger the freeze. The **Slider** control uses window subclassing to receive scroll messages, and this subclassing appears to create a reentrancy condition with certain COM interfaces that does not occur when the same call is made from other event sources. A `Sleep` delay before the COM call does not prevent the freeze.
>
> **Workaround:** decouple the COM call from the scroll event using a [**Timer**](../VB/Timer/) control. Record the slider value in the **Scroll** handler and perform the COM call in the **Timer** event instead. Use a reasonable interval (50 ms or more) --- a 1 ms interval that fires continuously can still trigger the freeze after several iterations. Alternatively, bypass the **Slider** control entirely and handle `WM_HSCROLL` / `WM_VSCROLL` with `TB_THUMBTRACK` via a direct `CreateWindowEx("msctls_trackbar32")` and a custom window procedure; this approach does not exhibit the freeze.

_Source threads: 1425710703863529492 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-10-09 to 2025-10-10_
_Reviewer note: The extracted finding tags this as VB.HScrollBar, but the thread title and content are explicitly about the WinNativeCommonCtls Slider control. Placed here on Slider.md. If the same freeze is confirmed to affect HScrollBar/VScrollBar (both also use subclassing), a parallel note should be added to docs/Reference/VB/HScrollBar/index.md and docs/Reference/VB/VScrollBar/index.md. The VBCCR slider was also confirmed to trigger the freeze, suggesting the root cause is scroll-event subclassing rather than anything tB-specific. Wayne Phillips (twinBASIC maintainer) confirmed the COM call never returns. Verify whether this has been fixed in a later tB release._

## docs/Reference/WinNativeCommonCtls/TreeView/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1107676681449254952]

## Per-node color and font formatting

The **TreeView** control does not expose properties for per-node foreground color, background color, or font. The underlying ComCtl32 control supports custom drawing through `WM_NOTIFY` / `NM_CUSTOMDRAW` notifications, so individual node formatting is achievable by subclassing the control's window handle ([**hWnd**](#hwnd)) and handling those messages directly in a Win32 callback.

An alternative that avoids subclassing is to use a WinRT XAML **TreeView** control, which natively supports per-node styling. This approach requires abandoning the Win32 form-based UI.

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/CodeEditor.md · after-remarks

## Code Editor Editing Commands

The IDE code editor provides several editing commands accessible from the right-click context menu or keyboard shortcuts:

- **Change All Occurrences** (Ctrl+F2) --- replaces every occurrence of the selected symbol name in the current module with a new name typed in-place.
- **Rename Symbol** --- available in the right-click context menu; performs a broader rename across the project. Availability and scope may vary by IDE version.
- **Code editor bookmarks** --- the editor supports setting bookmark markers on lines and jumping between them via the right-click menu or keyboard shortcuts. Bookmarks are scoped to the current editor session.
- **Last Position** (Ctrl+Shift+F2) --- navigates back through the History panel to the previous edit location or Go to Definition jump. Only edits and definition-navigation jumps create history entries; mouse clicks alone do not.

_Source threads: 1073564932181864488 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-02-10 to 2023-03-15_

The 'Rename Symbol' feature was only partially working as of early 2023 (showed a 'massage workplace edits' message); verify current behavior. The Last Position shortcut (Ctrl+Shift+F2) matches VB6. ## docs/Reference/tbIDE/KeyboardShortcuts.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1200571837684396112, 1358454331568820224, 1380480192459571314, 1220734616047059115, 1415707970875953340, 1428269371154890823]

> [!NOTE]
> **QWERTZ keyboard layouts (e.g. German) --- Undo and Redo shortcuts are reversed.** On QWERTZ keyboards the Y and Z keys are physically swapped relative to QWERTY, so the default Ctrl+Z (Undo) and Ctrl+Y (Redo) bindings fire in reverse. The fix is to create a custom keyboard shortcut group via **Window** menu > **Keyboard Shortcuts** > **Manage Keyboard Shortcuts**.
>
> To swap Undo and Redo so they match the physical QWERTZ positions:
>
> ```json
> {
>     "tbEditor_Undo":        ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Y"],
>     "tbEditor_Redo":        ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Z"],
>     "tbFormDesigner_Undo":  ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Y"],
>     "tbFormDesigner_Redo":  ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Z"]
> }
> ```
>
> Alternatively, to restore Ctrl+Z as Undo and reassign Ctrl+Y to delete the current line:
>
> ```json
> {
>     "tbEditor_Undo":         ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Z"],
>     "tbEditor_Redo":         [""],
>     "+tbEditor_DeleteLines": ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Y"]
> }
> ```
>
> A future release may include built-in shortcut groups for QWERTZ and other non-QWERTY layouts.

_Source threads: 1339638223655141506 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-02-13 to 2025-02-26_
_Reviewer note: This finding is about the IDE's built-in keyboard shortcut manager (the Window > Keyboard Shortcuts > Manage Keyboard Shortcuts UI), not the addin-SDK KeyboardShortcuts class documented on this page. Consider whether a dedicated Features/IDE page for the keyboard shortcut manager would be a better home. If so, move this note there and add a cross-reference from this page._

Press **Shift+F12** to open the IDE DevTools, go to the **Console** tab, and run `editor.getModel().getValue()`. ## docs/Reference/tbIDE/KeyboardShortcuts.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1200571837684396112, 1339638223655141506, 1358454331568820224, 1220734616047059115, 1415707970875953340, 1428269371154890823]

> [!NOTE]
> The [**Add**](#add) method registers shortcuts for addin-defined callbacks. To remap a **built-in IDE editor action** --- for example, to bind Ctrl+Y to Delete Line rather than Redo --- use the IDE's project-settings keyboard shortcut group mechanism instead. Create a custom shortcut group in the project settings file with a JSON object that maps action names to binding arrays. To move a key combination, the group must both assign the new binding **and** clear the old one; adding only the new binding is not enough because the existing binding in the default group still takes priority.
>
> Example --- remap Ctrl+Y from Redo to Delete Line:
>
> ```json
> {
>   "tbEditor_DeleteLines": ["{KEYDOWN}{KEYDOWNREPEAT}{CTRL}Y"],
>   "tbEditor_Redo": []
> }
> ```
>
> Setting an action's binding array to `[]` removes it from the default group. On non-US keyboard layouts, the physical key position --- not the key label --- may need to be used in the binding string.

_Source threads: 1380480192459571314 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-06-06_

Verify the project-settings JSON schema and the action name strings (tbEditor_DeleteLines, tbEditor_Redo) against the twinBASIC IDE source or documentation before publishing._

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/KeyboardShortcuts.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1200571837684396112, 1339638223655141506, 1358454331568820224, 1380480192459571314, 1415707970875953340, 1428269371154890823]

> [!NOTE]
> The `KeyboardShortcuts` class in the addin API registers *additional* shortcuts for addin callbacks. It cannot modify or remove the built-in IDE shortcuts. To disable or reassign a built-in shortcut, use the IDE's own shortcut scheme editor (**Window > Keyboard Shortcuts**): create a custom scheme, assign an empty string `""` to the command whose shortcut should be removed, and enable (tick) that scheme. For example, to unassign Ctrl+N from New Project and assign it to Next Bookmark instead, the custom scheme JSON should contain:
>
> ```json
> { "tbProject_New": [""], "tbEditor_NextBookmark": ["{KEYDOWN}{CTRL}N"] }
> ```
>
> The custom scheme must be enabled in **Window > Keyboard Shortcuts** for it to take effect. The built-in scheme cannot be edited directly.

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/Project.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1179138735338684519, 1220709824199921674, 1386403131302350989]

> [!NOTE]
> **Project.Save** dispatches the save command asynchronously to the compiler process. If the compiler process's save thread is blocked --- which can occur after the IDE has been open for an extended period --- the command is not processed and no error is raised. Two indicators confirm that a save completed: (1) the DEBUG CONSOLE prints two lines immediately after a successful save; if those lines do not appear, the save did not trigger; (2) the title bar shows a dot prefix before the project name when unsaved changes are present. If **Ctrl+S** (Save All) does not save, using the dedicated Save button on the toolbar may succeed.

When a save attempt fails due to a detectable I/O error (such as a full disk), the IDE retries the write up to five times with a one-second delay between attempts. After all retries are exhausted, a modal dialog appears prompting the user to choose a different save path. This retry behavior applies only to I/O errors raised during the disk write; it does not cover the case where the async save command is never dispatched to the compiler process.

_Source threads: 1101173674003935295 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-04-27 to 2023-05-12_
_Reviewer note: Verify against IDE source that the debug console prints exactly two lines on a successful save, and confirm the title-bar dot-prefix indicator is still current behavior. The retry count (5) and delay (1 s) should be checked against the IDE's disk-write implementation._

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/Project.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1101173674003935295, 1220709824199921674, 1386403131302350989]

> [!NOTE]
> The IDE's save facility operates in two stages: each dirty document is first saved in memory, and only after all dirty documents have been saved does the project persist to disk. If any document fails to save in the memory stage, the disk persist does not run. Under system memory pressure, Win32 file APIs (`WriteFile`) can report a successful write---with `lpNumberOfBytesWritten` matching the requested byte count---while the disk write-cache has not been flushed to disk. In this situation, success messages in the DEBUG CONSOLE (including `[EXPORT] COMPLETED (N folders, N files)` for projects configured to auto-export on save) do not guarantee that files were written to disk. Do not treat debug-console save or export messages as absolute confirmation that files are on disk when the system is under heavy memory load.

_Source threads: 1179138735338684519 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2023-11-28 to 2023-11-29_

Fixes were planned: checking the WriteFile return BOOL, read-back verification, and FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING. Verify whether these fixes shipped and whether the note should be softened or removed in a newer IDE version._

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/Themes.md · example

### Custom theme files

A custom theme file placed in `%APPDATA%\twinBASIC\themes\` can inherit from a built-in theme and override individual properties. Create a plain-text file with any name and the `.theme` extension. The first line specifies the base theme with `inherits:`, and each subsequent line sets one property:

```
inherits: Classic;
CodeIndentGuideVisible: 1;
```

Restart the IDE and select the new theme from the theme picker. The `CodeIndentGuideVisible` property controls the vertical indentation guide lines in the code editor.

> [!NOTE]
> The file format uses a semicolon after the value on each line. Any property not listed in the file takes its value from the inherited theme.

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1118729142448427071, 1141994321332154449, 1204475364118634596, 1209485371243765790, 1221458605920878763, 1222383214727790766, 1223210942276567111, 1223269020661186560, 1370280255100817448, 1467982883762340083, 1466743472315957363, 1072808702307999754, 1313972889266946089, 1336240314116997220, 1425373643919327293, 1428272192210210816, 1452844933156175874, 1465850804677120055, 1473716330606891313, 1152093758876295278, 1179926803666718730, 1252009603345022986, 1371497821252882572]

> [!NOTE]
> **Floating panel drag conflicts.** When a floating IDE panel's title bar is positioned over another draggable element --- a second panel's title bar, a Project Explorer file node, or a tab --- attempting to drag the floating panel to redock it faults immediately and the panel becomes invisible. The panel is not destroyed. To avoid this, first move the floating panel to a clear area of the IDE where its title bar does not overlap any other draggable element, then use the docking grab handle to redock it.
>
> If a panel becomes invisible after a failed drag, open the **View** menu and select the panel by name to restore it. A brief red highlight may appear before the panel reappears. If the View menu does not restore the panel, use **View → Restore Default Layout** or restart the IDE.

> [!NOTE]
> **Corrupt layout after saving during a panel transition.** Saving a custom IDE layout while a panel is simultaneously recorded in both the docked and the floating sections of the internal layout JSON --- a state that certain drag sequences can produce --- causes the panel to appear as a floating window with a blank, unclosable ghost panel in its former docked position on the next load. Save a fresh layout only after confirming that every panel is cleanly in one location. The IDE applies a defensive fix that discards a panel's floating-section entry when the same panel already appears in the docked section, but the underlying condition that creates the duplicate entry has not been fully resolved.

## Discovering IDE command names

Every twinBASIC IDE action has an internal command name. These names are usable as shortcut targets in the keyboard shortcut JSON configuration (see [**KeyboardShortcuts**](KeyboardShortcuts)).

To find a command name, hover the mouse over the corresponding toolbar button or menu item and look at the rightmost segment of the IDE status bar. Examples: `tbCompiler_Restart`, `tbBuild_Clean`, `tbBuild_Build`.

## Windows Forms vs. HTML tool windows

Add-ins can host standard Windows Forms rather than HTML/CSS tool windows. Some community add-ins use this approach and call the Win32 `SetParent()` API to make the form a child window of the IDE frame. However, HTML/CSS-based tool windows (created through [**ToolWindows.Add**](ToolWindows)) are the recommended approach for new add-ins: twinBASIC is planned to be cross-platform, and an add-in built on Windows Forms will not function on non-Windows platforms once that support is introduced.

Debugging add-ins is limited to tracelogging; interactive debug sessions are not supported for DLLs loaded into the IDE process.

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/index.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1118729142448427071, 1141994321332154449, 1200571837684396112, 1204475364118634596, 1209485371243765790, 1221458605920878763, 1222383214727790766, 1223210942276567111, 1223269020661186560, 1370280255100817448, 1467982883762340083, 1466743472315957363, 1072808702307999754, 1313972889266946089, 1336240314116997220, 1425373643919327293, 1428272192210210816, 1452844933156175874, 1465850804677120055, 1473716330606891313, 1152093758876295278, 1179926803666718730, 1252009603345022986]

> [!NOTE]
> The IDE loads addins from two locations: the `addins\Win32\` and `addins\Win64\` sub-folders of the IDE executable folder, and the matching sub-folders under `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\twinBASIC\addins\`. Files placed in the AppData location are preserved when the user installs a new version of the IDE. However, having the same addin file in both locations at the same time causes problems --- keep each addin DLL in one location only.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Which addins are visible depends on the bitness of the compiler background process, not on which project is open. The compiler process runs as 32-bit when the active project targets Win32 and as 64-bit when the project targets Win64. A 32-bit addin DLL will not appear when editing a Win64-target project, and vice versa.

_Source threads: 1371497821252882572 · confidence: high_
_Date range: 2025-05-12 to 2025-05-13_

## docs/Reference/tbIDE/index.md · new-section

## IDE registry entries

The list of recently opened projects shown in the IDE's New/Open dialog is stored in the Windows registry at:

```
HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\VB and VBA Program Settings\twinBASIC_IDE\RecentlyOpened
```

To clear obsolete entries in bulk, delete the values under that key using Registry Editor (`regedit.exe`) or a script. Individual entries can also be removed through the IDE's own UI.

_Source threads: 1511584056893112360 · confidence: high_

## docs/Reference/twinBASIC-Additions.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1427261753544409168]

### Command-line compilation

twinBASIC supports building projects from the command line without opening the IDE. Pass the path to a `.twinproj` file as the first argument, followed by one of two flags:

- `--buildAndExit32` --- compiles a 32-bit binary and exits.
- `--buildAndExit64` --- compiles a 64-bit binary and exits.

```
twinbasic.exe PathToProject.twinproj --buildAndExit64
```

> [!NOTE]
> Command-line compilation is preliminary. If a compile error occurs the process will exit without reporting an error code. This is sufficient for basic CI/CD automation but unsuitable where error detection and reporting is required.

## docs/Reference/twinBASIC-Additions.md · after-remarks [DUPLICATE? -- see also thread 1431348682271363182]

> [!NOTE]
>
> Unlike VB6, which always depends on `msvbvm60.dll` and carries the full cost of that runtime, twinBASIC includes only the code that a given project actually uses. Features such as the forms engine that are not referenced are not included in the output binary. This makes it possible to build very small native executables (under 20 KB for a minimal Win32 GUI project) without any size penalty for unused language features.

_Source threads: 1427261753544409168 · confidence: medium_
_Date range: 2025-10-14_

## docs/Reference/VBRUN/DataObject/GetFormat.md · after-remarks

> [!NOTE]
> Calling **GetFormat** inside an **OLEDragOver** event handler raises run-time error -2147467263 (0x80004001, E_NOTIMPL) when the drag originates from certain third-party applications. The error indicates that the underlying OLE data format query is not yet fully implemented for all drag sources. As a workaround, wrap the call in an `On Error Resume Next` block and treat an error as a **False** result.
